stages.title: Origin
stages.headline: Birth of Pesarattu in Andhra Pradesh
stages.narrative: Pesarattu is a traditional breakfast dish of Andhra Pradesh, made mainly from whole green gram (pesalu / green moong). The name comes from Telugu: pesara (green gram) + attu (pancake/dosa). It is a distinctive part of Andhra breakfast culture, traditionally eaten with spicy ginger chutney (Allam Pachadi). No reliable historical record gives the exact year, place or creator. Unlike regular dosa, the batter is not fermented; it is cooked right after grinding.

stages.title: Recipe
stages.headline: Pesarattu Recipe: 9 Steps
stages.narrative:
whole green gram (green moong), rice (optional, for extra crispness), ginger, green chillies, cumin seeds, salt, onion, fresh coriander leaves, cooking oil or ghee, ginger chutney (Allam Pachadi) for serving.

1. Wash and soak the green gram. - Soak in water for about 4 to 6 hours.
2. Drain the water. - Rinse the green gram once more.
3. Grind the batter. - Grind with ginger, green chillies, cumin and salt, adding a little water. It should be smooth and slightly thick.
4. Prepare the toppings. - Chop onions and coriander finely and keep ready.
5. Heat the pan. - Heat a dosa tawa and grease it lightly with oil.
6. Spread the batter. - Pour one ladle in the centre and spread in circles into a thin dosa.
7. Add the toppings. - Sprinkle onions and coriander and press in gently.
8. Cook until crisp. - Add a little oil around the edges. Cook until the bottom is golden brown and the edges lift.
9. Fold and serve. - Fold and serve hot with ginger chutney.

No fermentation needed. Cook right after grinding. A little rice in the batter gives extra crispness.

stages.title: Origin
stages.headline: Birth of Avakaya in Andhra Pradesh
stages.narrative: Avakaya (ఆవకాయ) is a traditional raw-mango pickle from Andhra Pradesh, also a long-standing tradition in Telugu homes of Telangana. The name joins "ava" (mustard) and "kaya" (raw fruit). It grew out of preserving sour raw mangoes in the summer mango season so they can be eaten through the year. Raw mango pieces are coated with mustard powder, red chilli powder and salt, then covered in gingelly (sesame) oil and matured in jars. It is a standard part of an Andhra meal, eaten with hot rice, dal and ghee. Making it is often a family activity every summer. No reliable record gives the exact year, place or creator of Avakaya.

Jars: Then - large ceramic jaadis (bharanis) filled by the whole family | Now - smaller jars for small home batches, kept bone-dry
Batch size: Then - big yearly batches shared across the family | Now - small batches of a few mangoes are common
Variations: Then - the classic mustard-chilli Avakaya | Now - many versions such as bellam (jaggery), nuvvu (sesame), allam (ginger), pesara (moong) and endu (sun-dried) avakaya
Where it comes from: Then - made only at home each summer | Now - also sold ready-made by pickle brands

stages.title: Recipe
stages.headline: Avakaya Recipe: 11 Steps
stages.narrative:
raw green sour mangoes, mustard seeds (sun-dried, ground fresh), red chilli powder, crystal salt (powdered), gingelly (sesame) oil, garlic cloves, fenugreek (methi) seeds, black chickpeas (optional, in place of garlic), hot rice with dal and ghee for serving.

1. Wash and soak the mangoes. - Use firm, sour raw mangoes. Soak them in water for about an hour.
2. Dry the pickle jar. - Wash it and sun-dry it fully. There must be no moisture at all.
3. Wipe and cut the mangoes. - Cut into pieces with the hard kernel kept on each piece. Remove the pith.
4. Dry the pieces. - Clean each piece with a soft cloth. Spread on a dry cloth for an hour or two.
5. Grind mustard and salt. - Grind sun-dried mustard seeds and crystal salt to a fine powder.
6. Make the spice mix. - Mix chilli powder, mustard powder and salt in equal weight. Add methi seeds, garlic and part of the oil. A fistful should hold its shape.
7. Coat the mango pieces. - Mix with clean, dry hands until every piece is coated.
8. Fill the jar. - Add the pieces with all the spice mix. Pour a little oil on top.
9. Seal and rest. - Close the lid and tie a cloth over it. Keep in a dry place and do not open for about 3 days.
10. Mix and top up. - On day 4, mix with a clean, dry ladle. Taste for salt. Add oil so a thin layer covers the pickle.
11. Mature and serve. - Mix again after another 4 days. Serve with hot rice, dal and ghee.

Always use a clean, dry spoon. Moisture spoils the pickle. Keep a thin layer of oil on top.

stages.narrative: Avakaya remains the crowning jewel of Telugu culinary heritage, eaten across Andhra Pradesh and Telangana with hot steamed rice, mudda pappu (thick toor dal) and generous ghee. While commercial brands now produce jarred versions, the summer ritual of making Avakaya at home in sun-dried ceramic jaadis remains a cherished living tradition.

stages.title: Origin
stages.headline: Birth of Thukpa in Arunachal Pradesh & the Himalayan Belt
stages.narrative: Thukpa traces back to eastern Tibetan noodle-and-broth traditions developed to combat freezing high-altitude mountain climates. The dish spread across ancient trans-Himalayan trade routes and Buddhist pilgrim trails into Arunachal Pradesh, becoming deeply anchored in the food culture of the Monpa community of Tawang and West Kameng. The exact date and individual creator are not documented with certainty, though regional chronicles record centuries of pastoral exchange. It is prepared in the slow-simmered broth infusion method, with Putang Thukpa—made with indigenous buckwheat noodles—being the cherished local Monpa specialty.

stages.title: Recipe
stages.headline: Thukpa Recipe: 10 Key Ingredients, 8 Steps
stages.narrative:
Key ingredients: handmade wheat noodles, chicken or pork, fresh ginger, mountain garlic, sliced onions, shredded cabbage and carrots, rich meat or vegetable stock, Sichuan pepper (yer ma), spring onions, mustard oil.

1. Boil the wheat noodles in salted water until just tender (al dente), drain thoroughly, rinse with cold water, and toss with a few drops of oil to prevent sticking.
2. Heat mustard oil in a heavy-bottomed pot over medium heat, then sauté finely chopped ginger and minced garlic until fragrant.
3. Add sliced onions and slit green chillies, sautéing for 2 minutes until soft and translucent.
4. Add the chicken or pork pieces, searing lightly for 3 to 4 minutes until evenly browned.
5. Pour in the rich stock, season with crushed Sichuan pepper (yer ma), turmeric, and salt, bringing the broth to a rolling boil.
6. Lower the heat, cover the pot with a lid, and simmer gently for 15 minutes so the meat tenderizes and infuses the soup.
7. Add the shredded cabbage and julienned carrots, simmering for 3 to 4 minutes until tender yet pleasantly crisp.
8. Place a portion of cooked noodles into warm serving bowls, ladle the piping-hot aromatic broth and vegetables over them, and garnish with spring onions.

stages.title: Origin
stages.headline: Birth of Bamboo Shoot Pork in Arunachal Pradesh & the Eastern Himalayas
stages.narrative: Bamboo shoot pork traces back to ancient ancestral foraging and hearth-cooking traditions of the indigenous hill communities of Arunachal Pradesh, notably the Adi, Nyishi, and Apatani peoples. In the dense montane forests, tender wild bamboo shoots were preserved through subterranean leaf fermentation (ekung, eup, and hikhu) to ensure year-round nourishment, while free-ranging country pork provided vital animal protein and fats during harsh winters. The exact date and individual creator are not documented with certainty, as food lore was transmitted orally across generations. It was traditionally cooked inside sealed green bamboo internodes over open wood fires or in heavy hearth pots, allowing the natural sourness of the shoots to tenderize the rich meat.

Cooking method: It was traditionally cooked inside sealed green bamboo internodes (penam arak) over open wood fires or simmered slowly in hearth pots without added oil or heavy spices.

stages.title: Recipe
stages.headline: Bamboo Shoot Pork Recipe: 10 Key Ingredients, 8 Steps
stages.narrative:
Key ingredients: pork belly or country pork, fermented bamboo shoots (ekung), fresh ginger, mountain garlic, fiery King Chilli or bird's eye chillies, wild mountain coriander, spring onions or wild greens, rock salt or indigenous tapyo salt, mustard oil, warm water.

1. Rinse the fermented bamboo shoots (ekung) lightly in cold water if intensely pungent; squeeze out excess brine and set aside.
2. Heat a splash of mustard oil in a heavy-bottomed iron pot or kadhai over medium flame, or add the pork directly so its fat renders naturally.
3. Add the pork pieces and sear over medium heat for 10 to 12 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the fat renders out and the meat turns lightly browned.
4. Reduce heat to medium-low, add coarsely pounded ginger and crushed mountain garlic, and sauté for 2 minutes until fragrant.
5. Add the slit King Chillies (or bird's eye chillies) and fermented bamboo shoots, stirring well to coat the shoots in the rendered pork fat.
6. Season with salt (or indigenous tapyo), pour in 1.5 cups of warm water to submerge the meat partially, and bring to a gentle boil.
7. Cover the pot with a tight lid and simmer on low heat for 35 to 45 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the pork is melt-in-the-mouth tender and the gravy reduces.
8. Uncover, fold in chopped wild mountain coriander and spring onions, rest for 5 minutes, and serve piping hot with steamed hill rice.

5. Add the slit King Chillies (or bird's eye chillies) and fermented bamboo shoots, stirring well to coat the shoots in the rendered pork fat.
6. Season with salt (or indigenous tapyo), pour in 1.5 cups of warm water to submerge the meat partially, and bring to a gentle boil.
7. Cover the pot with a tight lid and simmer on low heat for 35 to 45 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the pork is melt-in-the-mouth tender and the gravy reduces.
8. Uncover, fold in chopped wild mountain coriander and spring onions, rest for 5 minutes, and serve piping hot with steamed hill rice.

stages.title: Origin
stages.headline: Birth of Apong in Arunachal Pradesh & the Eastern Himalayas
stages.narrative: Apong traces back to ancient ancestral foraging and agricultural traditions of the indigenous hill communities of Arunachal Pradesh, notably the Adi, Nyishi, and Apatani peoples. Hand-harvested hill paddy was cooked and inoculated with wild medicinal herbal starter cakes (known as apop, epoh, or siye), cultivated through generations of botanical knowledge to induce natural fermentation. The exact date and individual creator are not documented with certainty, as brewing lore was passed down orally through women elders and hearth keepers. It was traditionally prepared as both a milky white brew (Pika Apong / Nogin) and a smoky dark brew using charred paddy husk ash (Poro Apong), serving as a sacred offering to deities and ancestors.

stages.title: Recipe
stages.headline: Apong Recipe: 10 Key Ingredients, 8 Steps
stages.narrative:
Key ingredients: indigenous hill rice, herbal fermentation starter cake (apop/epoh), wild medicinal starter herbs, paddy husk ash (taap/mikap), clean mountain spring water, wild banana leaves (oko leaves), woven bamboo filtration funnel (perop), traditional earthen fermentation pot, fermented rice mash, wild forest herbs.

1. Steam or boil the indigenous hill rice in a heavy pot until tender and fluffy, taking care that the grains remain distinct and not watery.
2. Spread the hot rice evenly across clean bamboo mats or wild banana leaves, allowing it to cool completely to room temperature so microbial cultures survive.
3. Grind the dried herbal starter cake (apop or epoh) into a fine powder using a traditional stone mortar.
4. Dust the powdered starter uniformly over the cooled rice (optionally incorporating charred paddy husk ash for dark Poro Apong), tossing thoroughly by hand.
5. Transfer the inoculated rice into a clean, dry earthen pot or leaf-lined container, pressing gently and covering the surface with fresh wild leaves.
6. Seal the mouth of the vessel securely and place it in a warm, undisturbed corner near the hearth for 5 to 7 days of solid-state fermentation.
7. Pour cool, pure spring water into the sweet, bubbly fermented rice mash and let it steep for 30 to 60 minutes to extract alcohol and natural sugars.
8. Strain the golden-cloudy liquid through a conical woven bamboo funnel (perop), collect the fresh brew in bamboo tumblers, and serve at room temperature.

stages.narrative: Litti Chokha traces back to the ancient agricultural and pastoral communities of the Gangetic plains of Bihar, where parched Bengal gram flour (sattu) has served for millennia as an imperishable, protein-dense travel ration. Peasant farmers and pastoralists encased spiced sattu inside coarse whole-wheat flour dough, baking the spheres directly in smoldering dried cow-dung (goitha or upla) ember pits while tending fields. Oral traditions and folklore also record its use as an essential, fuel-efficient battle ration by rebel soldiers under Veer Kunwar Singh during the 1857 uprising, as the stuffed dough balls required zero cooking vessels and lasted for days. Over centuries, the fire-charred litti became inextricably paired with chokha—a rustic mash of flame-roasted eggplant, potatoes, and tomatoes seasoned with raw mustard oil—and generously bathed in molten desi cow ghee.

Cultural significance: The quintessential soul food and culinary identity of Bihar, balancing wholesome roasted grains with smoky vegetable chokha and rich clarified butter.

stages.title: Recipe
stages.headline: Litti Chokha Recipe: 10 Key Ingredients, 8 Steps
stages.narrative:
Key ingredients: whole wheat flour (atta), roasted gram flour (sattu), large purple eggplant (baingan), ripe country tomatoes & potatoes, pure desi cow ghee, pungent cold-pressed mustard oil, ajwain (carom) & kalonji (nigella seeds), fresh garlic, ginger & green chillies, stuffed red chilli pickle masala, fresh coriander leaves & black rock salt.

1. In a large bowl, mix whole wheat flour with ajwain, salt, and 2 tablespoons of ghee or mustard oil; knead with water into a tight, firm dough and rest covered for 20 minutes.
2. In a separate bowl, blend sattu with finely chopped garlic, ginger, green chillies, ajwain, kalonji, spicy red chilli pickle masala (or amchur and lemon juice), coriander leaves, salt, and raw mustard oil until crumbly yet cohesive.
3. Divide dough into lemon-sized balls, hollow each into a deep cup, pack with 2 tablespoons of spiced sattu stuffing, pleat the edges to seal completely, and roll into smooth round spheres.
4. Slit the eggplant, insert garlic cloves into the cuts, and roast along with whole tomatoes directly over open flames until charred black and tender; boil and peel the potatoes.

stages.title: Origin
stages.headline: Birth of Thekua in Bihar & the Chhath Festival Tradition
stages.narrative: Thekua traces back to the ancient Sun-worship traditions and agricultural rhythms of Bihar, where it developed as the supreme, sacred mahaprasad of Chhath Puja—an ancient Vedic festival honoring Surya (the Sun God) and Chhathi Maiya. Revered across the Gangetic plains of Bihar, Jharkhand, eastern Uttar Pradesh, and the Terai region of Nepal, this festive delicacy was crafted from newly harvested autumn wheat flour, dark country sugarcane jaggery (gur), pure desi cow ghee, fennel seeds, and dry coconut. The semi-dry dough was traditionally hand-pressed onto intricately carved wooden moulds known as saancha, creating auspicious leaf, floral, and solar patterns before slow-frying in heavy iron kadhais over clay stoves. Its low moisture and high ghee content gave it remarkable natural preservation qualities, making it the essential travel ration and blessed token exchanged across families and pilgrim trails.

Historical background: Rooted in centuries-old Vedic solar worship and regional folklore; prepared with the strictest standards of ritual purity as the primary offering of Chhath Puja.
Regional food tradition: Embossed on hand-carved wooden moulds (saancha) and slow-fried in pure desi ghee over earthen stoves burning dried mango wood.
Cultural significance: The foremost cultural and festive sweet of Bihar, embodying deep spiritual devotion, familial sharing, and natural grain preservation.

stages.title: Recipe
stages.headline: Thekua Recipe: 10 Key Ingredients, 8 Steps
stages.narrative:
Key ingredients: coarse whole wheat flour (atta), sugarcane jaggery (gur), pure desi cow ghee, dry coconut slices (sukha nariyal), fennel seeds (saunf), green cardamom powder, semolina (sooji), white sesame seeds, filtered warm water, ghee or oil for deep frying.

1. Dissolve chopped sugarcane jaggery in 1/2 cup of warm water, stirring until melted completely, then strain through a fine sieve to remove any sediment and allow to cool.
2. In a wide mixing bowl (parat), combine coarse whole wheat flour and semolina, then add warm melted desi cow ghee.
3. Rub the ghee thoroughly into the flour with your fingertips for 4 to 5 minutes until the mixture resembles coarse sand and holds together when pressed in your palm.
4. Fold in thinly sliced dry coconut, fennel seeds, crushed green cardamom powder, and white sesame seeds, tossing to distribute evenly throughout the flour.
5. Gradually sprinkle the cooled jaggery water over the flour, pressing and gathering it into a very tight, stiff, crumbly dough without over-kneading.
6. Divide into lemon-sized portions, shape between palms into smooth cylindrical rolls, and press firmly onto a greased carved wooden mould (saancha) to emboss leaf or sunburst patterns.
7. Heat ghee or oil in a heavy iron kadhai over medium flame, then reduce heat to low-medium (150°C–160°C) and gently slide in 4 to 5 thekuas.
8. Fry patiently on gentle heat for 10 to 12 minutes, turning once golden-brown and firm, drain on paper towels, cool completely to crisp perfection, and store in an airtight container for up to 3 weeks.

stages.title: Origin
stages.headline: Birth of Silao Khaja in Nalanda & the Ancient Magadhan Route
stages.narrative: Silao Khaja traces back to the ancient town of Silao, nestled between the historic ruins of Nalanda Mahavihara and the royal hill-girt capital of Rajgir in Bihar. Long documented as a vibrant stop along ancient trade and pilgrimage highways, Silao developed a celebrated artisanal sweet-making tradition that dates back centuries. Local folklore and oral histories connect the layered delicacy to Buddhist-era pilgrims, travellers, and monks traversing the Magadhan empire, with popular legends recounting that Lord Buddha was offered khaja on his journey through the region. Master confectioners (halwais) developed an exquisite multi-layered pastry consisting of up to 52 paper-thin sheets of wheat dough folded with clarified butter, deep-fried until crisp and dipped in clear sugar syrup. In December 2018, this unique cultural sweet was formally awarded the Geographical Indication (GI) Tag, cementing Silao's status as the historic birthplace of authentic Bihar khaja.

Historical background: Anchored in centuries-old sweet-making lineages; oral traditions connect its origins to ancient Magadhan travellers, celebrated in December 2018 with a formal GI Tag.
Regional food tradition: Multi-layered pastry consisting of up to 52 microscopic sheets laminated with pure ghee, slow-fried in cast-iron kadhais, and glazed in warm cardamom sugar syrup.
Cultural significance: The pride of Nalanda gastronomy, revered for its feather-light, crispy flakiness and deep association with regional hospitality and pilgrimage customs.

stages.title: Recipe
stages.headline: Silao Khaja Recipe: 10 Key Ingredients, 8 Steps
stages.narrative:
Key ingredients: refined wheat flour (maida), pure desi ghee, granulated white sugar, green cardamom powder, rice flour (for saata layering paste), filtered water, few drops of lemon juice, pinch of sea salt, rose or kewra water, ghee or oil for deep frying.

1. In a large bowl, mix refined flour (maida) with a pinch of salt and 3 tablespoons of warm melted ghee, rubbing between fingertips until it resembles fine breadcrumbs.
2. Gradually add chilled water and knead into a smooth, firm, pliable dough, covering with a damp muslin cloth to rest for 30 minutes.
3. In a small bowl, whisk 4 tablespoons of melted ghee with 2 tablespoons of rice flour or fine maida until smooth and creamy to prepare the lamination paste (saata).
4. Divide rested dough into equal balls; roll each out on a clean dusted marble surface into a paper-thin, translucent rectangular sheet.
5. Smear a delicate, uniform layer of saata paste over the sheet, stack a second rolled sheet on top, apply more paste, and repeat with 4 to 5 sheets before rolling tightly into a compact Swiss-roll log.
6. Cut the log crosswise into 1.5-inch segments, then flatten each segment lengthwise with a single gentle stroke of the rolling pin to separate the 52 microscopic layers.
7. Heat ghee or oil in a heavy-bottomed kadhai over medium flame, lower to gentle heat (140°C–150°C), and fry khajas slowly for 12 to 15 minutes, basting with hot fat until the layers fan open and turn pale golden.
8. Prepare a light one-string sugar syrup with sugar, water, green cardamom, and lemon juice; immerse hot drained khajas for 30 to 45 seconds, transfer to a wire rack to set, and store in an airtight container for up to 2 weeks.

stages.title: Origin
stages.headline: Birth of Chila in Chhattisgarh & the Mahanadi Basin
details: Origin in the Mahanadi Basin: Known as the rice bowl of central India, Chhattisgarh has cultivated thousands of indigenous rice landraces for millennia. Chila (locally pronounced Chilha) evolved as an essential indigenous peasant breakfast crafted from freshly harvested rice.

Tribal & agricultural festivals: Chila holds deep cultural sanctimony during agrarian festivals such as Hareli (celebrating agricultural tools and monsoon crops) and Pola (venerating bullocks and livestock), where women prepare baskets of chilas as festive offerings.

Historical documentation: Folk oral traditions and regional Chhattisgarhi lore document chila as an ancient, unfermented quick crepe baked by rural households before heading to work in lush paddy fields.

Cooking method: Traditionally poured onto a heated earthen or rough-hewn cast-iron griddle (lohe ka tawa) over a wood-fire hearth, gently swirled thin with a leaf or wooden paddle, and roasted with minimal indigenous oil.

stages.title: Recipe
stages.headline: Chila Recipe: 10 Key Ingredients, 8 Steps
chips: Roasted tomato and green garlic chutney (for serving)
details: Key ingredients: rice flour (chawal ka atta), filtered water, cumin seeds (jeera), finely chopped green chillies, finely chopped fresh coriander, finely chopped onions (optional), white sesame seeds (til), mustard oil or ghee (for roasting), rock salt (sendha namak), roasted tomato and green garlic chutney (for serving).
1. In a wide mixing bowl, whisk 1.5 cups of fresh fine rice flour with rock salt, cumin seeds, finely chopped green chillies, and fresh coriander leaves.
2. Gradually pour 1.5 to 2 cups of filtered water in batches, whisking continuously to form a smooth, lump-free, free-flowing batter of pouring consistency similar to dosa or buttermilk.
3. Cover the bowl with a clean cloth and let the batter rest for 10 to 15 minutes, allowing the rice starch to hydrate evenly.
4. Heat a heavy seasoned cast-iron flat griddle (tawa) on medium flame until hot; lightly grease the surface using a halved onion dipped in mustard oil or ghee.

5. Stir the rested batter well from the bottom, pour a generous ladleful (about 1/2 cup) onto the centre of the hot tawa, and gently swirl or tilt the pan outwards to spread it into a thin circular round.
6. Optionally sprinkle a pinch of white sesame seeds or finely diced onions across the moist top surface, and drizzle a few drops of mustard oil around the circumference.
7. Cook undisturbed on medium-low heat for 2 to 3 minutes until the underside turns crisp, golden-brown, and the edges naturally release from the tawa.

8. Flip gently with a thin spatula, roast the other side for 1 to 2 minutes until lightly speckled, fold into a half-moon, and serve piping hot alongside tangy roasted green tomato (tamatar-mirchi) chutney or spicy bathua dal.

details: Origin in tribal heartlands: Fara (often called Farra or Muthiya) is an indigenous steamed dumpling deeply rooted in the rural and tribal culinary traditions of Chhattisgarh, born from the abundant harvests of indigenous paddy.
Festive importance: Central to harvest celebrations including Hareli, Teeja, and Pitru Paksha, where steamed rice confections are prepared as sacred offerings and wholesome family sustenance.

Historical documentation: Mentioned in regional ethnographic chronicles and local folklore of central India as a zero-waste, protein-rich innovation combining local rice flour with indigenous wild or farm-grown pulses.
Cooking method: Prepared by hand-shaping rice dough around seasoned lentil mash, steaming in perforated earthenware over bubbling pots, and lightly crisping with mustard seeds in a cast-iron skillet.

stages.title: Recipe
stages.headline: Fara Recipe: 10 Key Ingredients, 8 Steps
chips: Mustard oil or ghee (for dough and tempering)
details: Key ingredients: fresh rice flour (chawal atta), bengal gram lentils (chana dal), split black gram lentils (urad dal), green chillies and fresh ginger, garlic cloves (lahsun), mustard seeds (sarson / rai), fresh curry leaves (kadi patta), white sesame seeds (safed til), fresh coriander leaves, mustard oil or ghee (for dough and tempering).

1. Rinse and soak chana dal and urad dal in warm water for 4 hours; drain thoroughly and grind coarsely in a stone mortar or mixer with green chillies, ginger, garlic, cumin, and rock salt without adding water.
2. Fold chopped fresh coriander leaves into the coarse spiced dal mixture to form the savoury stuffing; set aside in a cool bowl.
3. In a saucepan, bring 1.5 cups of water to a rolling boil with 1/2 teaspoon of salt and 1 teaspoon of mustard oil or ghee.
4. Gradually pour the boiling water into 1.5 cups of fine rice flour, stirring briskly with a wooden spoon, cover with a lid, and rest for 10 minutes to let the rice flour steam-cook.
5. Once comfortably warm, knead the mixture vigorously for 3 to 4 minutes into a pliable, smooth, non-sticky rice dough; grease palms lightly with oil.

6. Pinch off lemon-sized dough portions, roll into smooth rounds, flatten between palms into 3-inch discs, place a spoonful of dal stuffing in the centre, and fold over into crescent or cylindrical dumplings, pinching edges to seal partially.
7. Arrange dumplings onto a greased perforated steamer plate and steam covered over vigorous boiling water for 12 to 15 minutes until the dough turns glossy, translucent, and firm to the touch.

8. Heat mustard oil in a wide pan, crackle mustard seeds, curry leaves, slit green chillies, and white sesame seeds; gently toss the steamed faras until golden and lightly crisped, serving hot with fiery roasted tomato chutney.

stages.narrative: Dhokla is a steamed, fermented savoury cake from Gujarat, now eaten across India. A pulse-based dish called dukkia, seen as a precursor, is mentioned in a Jain text dated to the 11th century (sources give 1066 or 1068 CE). The word “dhokla” itself appears in the Gujarati text Varanaka Samuchaya, dated to about 1520 CE. The traditional version uses a fermented batter of rice and split chickpeas (chana dal), steamed rather than fried. The exact creator and date are not documented, so treat dukkia as a likely ancestor rather than the same dish. Khaman, made entirely from chickpea batter, is a related but separate preparation.
details: Origin in Gujarat: rice and chana dal soaked and ground, fermented, then steamed in slabs.
Historical precursor: A pulse-based dish called dukkia is mentioned in an 11th-century Jain text (1066 or 1068 CE).
Literary reference: The word 'dhokla' appears in the Gujarati text Varanaka Samuchaya, dated to c. 1520 CE.
Cooking method: Steaming, not frying, with fermentation giving the sour taste and sponge.
stages.evidenceNote: Wikipedia, 'Dhokla'; K. T. Achaya, A Historical Dictionary of Indian Food; Knocksense (Ahmedabad), 'Steaming through centuries'.

stages.title: Recipe
stages.headline: Dhokla Recipe: 8 Steps
stages.narrative:
besan (gram flour), curd, ginger–green chilli paste, turmeric, salt, sugar, lemon juice, fruit salt (Eno), oil with mustard seeds, curry leaves and coriander.

1. Mix besan, curd, ginger–green chilli paste, turmeric, salt, sugar and lemon juice with water into a smooth, pourable batter. Rest it for about 10 minutes.
2. Heat water in a steamer and grease a tray with oil.
3. Add fruit salt to the batter just before cooking and stir gently, once, until it froths.
4. Pour the batter into the greased tray straight away.
5. Steam on medium heat for about 15 minutes, until a skewer comes out clean.
6. Let it cool slightly, then cut into squares.
7. Heat oil, crackle mustard seeds, add green chillies and curry leaves, then pour in a little water and sugar. Pour this tempering over the dhokla.
8. Garnish with coriander and grated coconut and serve with green chutney and fried chillies.

stages.title: Origin
stages.headline: Birth of Undhiyu in Gujarat
stages.narrative: Undhiyu (also spelled undhiyo or oondhiya) is a mixed winter-vegetable dish of Gujarat, closely tied to Surat. Its name comes from the Gujarati word undhu, "upside down", because the pot was traditionally buried upside down with fire on top. One account says it evolved from umbadiyo, a southern Gujarat dish cooked in a buried pit; this is a "said to" claim, not documented fact. Surti papdi (flat green beans) is its base, and it is cooked from November to February, when its vegetables are in season. It is the dish most associated with Uttarayan, the kite-flying harvest festival. No creator or date is documented.
details: Origin in Gujarat: vegetables and spice mix packed in the pot with no water, buried upside down, and cooked in their own juices for about 3 to 4 hours.
Traditional cookware: Earthen pot (matlu or matla), coated with mud and sealed.
Traditional heat source: Pit in the ground with lit charcoal or embers layered over the upturned pot.
Cooking method: Slow indirect heat from above, giving a smoky flavour.
stages.evidenceNote: Harper's Bazaar India, “Decoding the many layers and flavours of undhiyo”; Knocksense (Ahmedabad), traditional preparation of undhiyu; Tarla Dalal, Surti undhiyu.

stages.title: Evolution of Food
stages.headline: Evolution of Food: Then vs Now
stages.narrative:
Undhiyu moved from a buried earthen pot cooked for hours over charcoal to gas stoves, pressure cookers and restaurant reinventions, while village kitchens still make the matla version.

Vessel: Then - Sealed earthen pot (matlu or matla), coated with mud | Now - Large vessels, pressure cookers and non-stick pans
Heat source: Then - Pit with charcoal or embers on top | Now - Gas stove
Cooking time: Then - About 3 to 4 hours | Now - Two pressure-cooker whistles, then a short finish on low heat
Water: Then - None; vegetables cook in their own juices | Now - A little hot water added (about 2 cups in one recipe)
Flavour: Then - Smoky, from indirect heat | Now - Fresh green masala; less smoke
Oil: Then - More oil in the traditional method | Now - Pressure-cooker version uses less oil and can turn dry
Regional styles: Then - Village matla undhiyo | Now - Surat (garlic-heavy), Ahmedabad (spicier, oilier), Kathiyawadi (spices only, no green masala)
Reinventions: Then - Home and festival dish | Now - Restaurants offer a baked oil-free version, a Jain version and an undhiyo okonomiyaki

stages.title: Recipe
stages.headline: Undhiyu Recipe: 8 Steps
stages.narrative:
Surti papdi, purple yam and yam, baby potatoes, raw banana, small black brinjals, fresh toovar seeds, muthiya (fenugreek dumplings), coconut-coriander green masala with green garlic, ginger–green chilli paste, and oil with carom seeds and asafoetida.

1. Make the muthiya: squeeze salted chopped methi leaves, mix with wheat flour, besan, ginger–green chilli paste, sugar, turmeric, chilli powder and oil into a soft dough. Shape 18 to 20 pieces and deep fry on medium heat until golden. They can be made a day ahead.
2. Mix the green masala by hand: grated coconut, coriander, green garlic, coriander-cumin powder, ginger–green chilli paste, chilli powder, sugar, lemon juice and salt. It should taste spicy and sweet.
3. Slit the baby potatoes, brinjals and raw banana without separating the segments, and stuff them with about half the masala.
4. Combine the surti papdi, purple yam, yam and toovar seeds with the remaining masala. Rest for 8 to 10 minutes.
5. Heat oil in a pressure cooker, add carom seeds, asafoetida and a pinch of soda bicarbonate, then add the stuffed potatoes and brinjals, followed by the marinated vegetables.
6. Add salt and about 2 cups hot water, mix gently and pressure cook on high for 2 whistles. Let the steam release before opening.
7. Move to a large non-stick pan, add the stuffed bananas and muthiya, and cook on low heat, stirring gently, until the bananas are tender.
8. Serve hot, garnished with coriander, with poori and shrikhand.

stages.title: Origin & History
stages.headline: Handvo in the food geography of Gujarat
stages.narrative: Gujarat's trading coast and dry interior created a largely vegetarian cuisine of fermented batters, pulses, winter vegetables and a sweet–sour balance. Handvo is a fermented or steamed preparation associated with Gujarati household kitchens of the Ahmedabad–Surat belt. A fermented savoury cake that uses leftover dals and seasonal gourd, often made for travel and fasting-adjacent meals. The dish is documented in regional cookery and food writing, but no securely dated earliest written reference has been established for it; this atlas therefore claims no century of invention.
details: Geographical & cultural origin: Gujarati household kitchens of the Ahmedabad–Surat belt, in Gujarat.

Historical background: The dish is documented in regional cookery and food writing, but no securely dated earliest written reference has been established for it; this atlas therefore claims no century of invention.
Regional food tradition: A fermented savoury cake that uses leftover dals and seasonal gourd, often made for travel and fasting-adjacent meals.

Cultural significance: A naturally fermented batter of rice, mixed dals and grated bottle gourd, baked or shallow-steamed in a mould until the crust is deep gold, then crackled with a mustard-sesame tempering.

stages.title: Recipe & Making
stages.headline: How Handvo is made
stages.narrative: The defining technique is Rice and mixed pulses are soaked, ground and fermented with curd, then baked or steamed in a greased mould with a mustard–sesame crackle on top. Soaking, grinding, fermenting, kneading, stuffing or tempering is done in the order the recipe requires; Grain or pulse batters are soaked, stone- or mixer-ground and left to ferment with ambient lactic microflora before steaming in moulds, leaves or steamers. Steel steamers and packaged batter now replace earthen pots.

stages.title: Origin
stages.headline: Birth of Bajra Khichdi in Haryana & Harappan Agrarian Antiquity
details: Ancient millet hearths: Pearl millet (bajra) has been cultivated across the semi-arid plains of Haryana and the Ghaggar-Hakra valley since Harappan and Vedic times, providing robust sustenance through harsh northern winters.

Pastoral & agrarian lifestyle: Haryana's traditional farming community relied on bajra khichdi as a slow-burning source of warmth, stamina, and nutrition during freezing winter nights and long days in the fields.

Historical documentation: Mentioned in historical Punjabi and Haryanvi agricultural chronicles as the staple evening meal of rural homesteads, prepared as the wood-fire chulha burned low after cooking flatbreads.
Cooking method: Pounded meticulously in deep stone mortars (okhli) using heavy iron-ringed pestles (musal) to strip the tough fibrous outer skin, then slow-simmered in earthen pots over dying embers.

stages.title: Recipe
stages.headline: Bajra Khichdi Recipe: 10 Key Ingredients, 8 Steps
chips: Finely chopped green chillies and ginger
Freshly churned white butter (desi makkhan) / Jaggery (gur) (for serving)
details: Key ingredients: whole pearl millet (bajra), yellow split moong dal (dhuli moong), pure desi cow ghee, cumin seeds (jeera), asafoetida (hing), turmeric powder (haldi), finely chopped green chillies and ginger, rock salt (sendha namak), filtered water, freshly churned white butter (desi makkhan) / jaggery (gur) (for serving).

1. Sprinkle 2 tablespoons of warm water over whole bajra grains in a bowl, let rest for 10 minutes to loosen the fibrous outer husk, then pulse lightly in a stone mortar (okhli) or food processor and blow away the husk.
2. Coarsely pound or pulse the de-husked bajra into broken grits (dalia texture); rinse yellow split moong dal thoroughly and soak together with the broken bajra in warm water for 30 minutes.
3. Heat 2 tablespoons of pure desi cow ghee in a heavy-bottomed clay handi or deep cooker over medium flame.
4. Add cumin seeds and let them splutter; add a generous pinch of asafoetida (hing), grated ginger, and finely chopped green chillies, sauteing for 30 seconds until aromatic.
5. Add turmeric powder and rock salt, then drain and add the soaked bajra and moong dal grits, sauteing in the hot spiced ghee for 2 minutes to toast the grains.
6. Pour in 4 to 5 cups of hot filtered water, stirring vigorously with a wooden churner (madhani) to prevent any lump formation.

7. Bring to a rolling boil, then lower flame to low, cover with a tight lid, and simmer gently for 25 to 30 minutes (or pressure-cook for 4 to 5 whistles on medium-low), stirring occasionally until the grains are meltingly tender and creamy.

8. Rest covered for 5 minutes, mash lightly with the back of a ladle, spoon into clay bowls, crown with a generous dollop of freshly churned white butter (makkhan), and serve steaming hot with chilled spiced buttermilk or sugarcane jaggery.

stages.title: Origin
stages.headline: Birth of Kadhi Pakora in Haryana Pastoral Dairy Heartland
details: Pastoral dairy heritage: With Haryana's legendary dairy culture celebrated for the prized Murrah buffalo and dairy cows, sour buttermilk (chaas) has always been churned in abundance every morning in every village courtyard.

The culinary logic of 'kadhna': The word 'Kadhi' originates from the Hindi verb 'kadhna', meaning to simmer patiently over low heat for hours. Slow simmering curd with gram flour prevented curdling while imparting a rich velvet consistency.

Historical documentation: Rooted in centuries-old rural culinary practices documented across Haryana, Punjab, and western Uttar Pradesh, where kadhi served as the hearty companion to wheat and pearl millet rotis.

Cooking method: Slowly simmered in large brass or iron cauldrons over low-burning hearth embers, studded with crispy deep-fried onion and spinach pakoras, and finished with a sizzling ghee-spiced tempering.

stages.title: Recipe
stages.headline: Kadhi Pakora Recipe: 10 Key Ingredients, 8 Steps
chips: Finely sliced onions and spinach (for pakoras)
Rock salt (sendha namak) and fresh coriander
details: Key ingredients: sour whole-milk curd (dahi / chaas), bengal gram flour (besan), pure desi cow ghee, fenugreek seeds (methi dana), cumin and mustard seeds, asafoetida (hing), finely sliced onions and spinach (for pakoras), dried whole red chillies, turmeric and red chilli powder, rock salt (sendha namak) and fresh coriander.

1. In a deep earthen or stainless pot, vigorously whisk 2 cups of thick sour curd (or churned buttermilk) with 1/2 cup of gram flour (besan), turmeric powder, and 4 cups of water until completely smooth, silky, and free of lumps.

2. In a mixing bowl, prepare the pakora batter by combining 1 cup of besan, sliced onions, shredded spinach, green chillies, carom seeds (ajwain), a pinch of hing, salt, and water into a thick, fluffy drop-consistency batter, whisking briskly for 3 minutes to aerate.

3. Heat mustard oil or ghee in a kadhai, drop small lemon-sized spoonfuls of pakora batter into medium-hot fat, and deep-fry patiently for 5 to 6 minutes until crispy, golden-brown, and cooked through; drain on paper towels.
4. Place the pot of curd-besan mixture on medium-high heat, stirring continuously in one direction until it comes to a vigorous first boil to prevent the curd from splitting.
5. Lower the flame to low and let the kadhi simmer gently (kadhna) uncovered for 35 to 45 minutes, stirring periodically as it thickens and develops a rich, tangy depth of flavour.

6. Gently drop the warm crispy pakoras into the simmering kadhi, season with rock salt, and simmer for another 8 to 10 minutes so the pakoras absorb the tangy gravy while retaining their soft, spongy texture.

7. In a small tadka pan, heat 2 tablespoons of desi cow ghee; add fenugreek seeds (methi dana), cumin seeds, mustard seeds, broken whole dried red chillies, and asafoetida, letting them crackle until deeply fragrant.

8. Pour the sizzling red ghee tadka immediately over the simmering kadhi, cover with a tight lid for 2 minutes to trap the aromatic vapours, garnish with fresh coriander, and serve hot with bajra roti, steamed basmati rice, or churma.

stages.headline: Birth of Haryanvi Churma in Haryana Agrarian & Pehelwan Traditions
details: Agrarian & wrestling heartland: Renowned throughout the rural belts of Rohtak, Jhajjar, Sonipat, and Jind, Churma is the supreme emblem of Haryana's legendary 'Doodh-Dahi ka Khana' diet that has powered generations of farmers and wrestlers (pehelwans).

Celebratory & harvest role: Prepared during auspicious occasions, family reunions, childbirth ceremonies, and harvest festivals, churma represents heartfelt maternal hospitality and rustic agricultural bounty.

Historical documentation: Documented in regional folk songs (Raginis) and oral literature of Haryana as the essential wholesome confection carried by travellers, warriors, and youth training in traditional akharas.

stages.title: Recipe
stages.headline: Haryanvi Churma Recipe: 10 Key Ingredients, 8 Steps
chips: Unrefined sugarcane jaggery (gur) / Shakkar or Khand
details: Key ingredients: coarse whole wheat flour (atta), pure desi cow ghee, unrefined sugarcane jaggery (gur) / shakkar or khand, green cardamom powder (elaichi), finely chopped almonds and cashews, dry melon seeds (magaz), warm full-fat milk, warm filtered water (for dough), pinch of rock salt, edible dry ginger powder (sonth).
1. In a wide kneading platter (parat), combine 2 cups of coarse whole wheat flour with a pinch of rock salt and 2 tablespoons of melted warm desi cow ghee.
2. Rub the ghee into the flour with fingertips for 2 minutes, then gradually knead with warm water or milk into a stiff, firm dough; cover with a damp cloth and rest for 15 minutes.
3. Divide the rested dough into 3 to 4 large portions and roll each into a thick 1/2-inch flatbread (moti roti), piercing the surface with fingertips or a fork to ensure even heat penetration.

4. Roast the thick roti on a heavy iron tawa over low-medium heat, pressing gently with a clean cotton cloth until brown spots appear; finish directly over open flame or hearth embers until crisp, blistered, and thoroughly cooked inside.

5. While the thick rotis are steaming hot, immediately tear them into small chunks into a wide parat, and crush vigorously by hand (or pulse in brief intervals in a stone mortar or mixer) into fine, even crumbs.
6. Grate or crush soft sugarcane jaggery (or measure unrefined desi shakkar/khand) and mix thoroughly into the warm crushed wheat crumbs so it begins to melt from the residual heat.

7. Warm 1/2 cup to 3/4 cup of pure desi cow ghee in a pan; lightly toast melon seeds (magaz), chopped almonds, and cashews, then pour the hot ghee and nuts along with green cardamom powder directly over the mixture.

8. Knead the mixture vigorously with both palms for 3 to 5 minutes until the ghee binds the sweetened crumbs into a luscious, aromatic crumble; shape into round laddoos or serve loose in clay bowls alongside cold fresh milk or spicy kadhi.

stages.title: Origin
stages.headline: Birth of Siddu in Himachal Pradesh & the Western Himalayas
details: Origin in the Western Himalayas: Deeply embedded in the high-altitude valleys of Kullu, Mandi, Shimla, and Kangra, Siddu evolved as a dense, high-calorie steamed bread designed to provide warmth and stamina during freezing Himalayan winters.

Cultural & festive significance: Traditionally prepared during local winter festivals, family weddings, and festive gatherings such as Diwali and Lohri, where piping hot steamed bread drenched in pure cow ghee serves as the supreme gesture of mountain hospitality.

Historical documentation: Folkloric oral traditions and regional Himalayan chronicles record the ancient practice of leavening whole wheat dough with wild natural yeast (khameer) and stuffing it with foraged poppy seeds, wild hemp, or walnuts.

Cooking method: Hand-shaped into plump oval or crescent pockets around seasoned nut or pulse paste, rested for secondary proofing, and steamed over boiling water in traditional layered copper or brass steamers.

stages.title: Recipe
stages.headline: Siddu Recipe: 10 Key Ingredients, 8 Steps
details: Key ingredients: whole wheat flour (atta), active dry yeast / indigenous starter, poppy seeds (khus khus), crushed walnuts (akhrot), finely chopped green chillies, fresh ginger paste, fresh coriander leaves, warm filtered water or milk, rock salt (sendha namak), pure desi cow ghee (for serving).
1. In a small bowl, dissolve 1 teaspoon of yeast and a pinch of sugar in 1/4 cup of lukewarm water or milk; let stand for 10 minutes until frothy and bubbly.
2. In a large mixing platter, combine 2 cups of whole wheat flour with 1/2 teaspoon of salt and the activated yeast mixture, gradually adding lukewarm water to knead a soft, pliable, smooth dough.
3. Coat the dough with a few drops of oil or ghee, cover with a warm damp cloth, and let rise in a warm spot for 1.5 to 2 hours until doubled in volume.
4. Soak poppy seeds (khus khus) in warm water for 2 hours, drain completely, and grind into a coarse thick paste with walnuts, green chillies, ginger paste, rock salt, and chopped coriander leaves.
5. Punch down the fermented dough, divide into 4 equal balls, and roll each ball on a dusted board into a 5-inch round disc about 1/4-inch thick.
6. Place 2 tablespoons of the poppy seed-walnut stuffing onto one half of the dough disc, fold the other half over to form a crescent half-moon, and firmly crimp or twist the edges to seal.
7. Arrange the stuffed siddus on greased perforated steamer plates, cover, and let rest for 10 minutes for secondary rising while bringing the steamer water to a rapid rolling boil.

8. Steam covered over high heat for 15 to 18 minutes until the dough turns firm, glossy, and sounds hollow when tapped; slice open hot, pour generous spoonfuls of hot melted desi ghee into the centre, and serve with mint-coriander chutney or spicy dal.

details: Origin in royal Chamba & Kangra: Traditionally said to have originated around the 10th century CE under King Jaistambh of Chamba, who was inspired by Kashmiri royal feasts to create a multi-course vegetarian temple banquet dedicated to Lord Shiva.

The hereditary Boti guild: Cooked exclusively by hereditary Brahmin culinary masters known as 'Botis', who observe sacred purity, passing down precise spice measurements and cooking sequences across generations.
Community pangat tradition: Served during weddings, auspicious religious festivals, and community celebrations to guests seated in egalitarian rows (pangat) directly on fresh leaf plates (pattals).

Cooking method: Prepared strictly without onion, garlic, or tomatoes, slow-simmered in colossal narrow-mouthed heavy brass or bronze cauldrons (charotis) nested in deep wood-fire earthen trench ovens (chulhas).

chips: Dried tamarind pulp or amchur (for khatta)
Sugarcane jaggery or sugar (for mitha bhaat)

details: Key ingredients: basmati rice, kabuli chickpeas (chana) / rajma, split black gram (maah ki dal), thick whole-milk curd (dahi), pure desi cow ghee, dried tamarind pulp or amchur (for khatta), sugarcane jaggery or sugar (for mitha bhaat), whole spices (cloves, cardamom, cinnamon), dry ginger powder (saunth) and fennel seeds, mustard oil and rock salt.
1. Soak chickpeas (or Chamba rajma) and split black gram (maah ki dal) overnight in separate bowls of water; rinse thoroughly.
2. Boil chickpeas in lightly salted water with black cardamom and cinnamon until completely tender and creamy; drain and reserve stock.
3. In a heavy-bottomed brass pot or deep pan, heat pure desi cow ghee over medium heat and crackle cloves, cinnamon, green cardamom, and bay leaves until aromatic.
4. Lower flame and gradually whisk in 2 cups of thick beaten curd, stirring continuously in one direction for 15 minutes to prevent splitting until ghee separates and the gravy turns golden.
5. Fold the boiled chickpeas, dry ginger powder (saunth), fennel powder, turmeric, and rock salt into the curd gravy, simmering on gentle heat for 20 minutes to make the signature Chana Madra.
6. In a second pot, simmer split black gram (maah ki dal) with mustard oil, hing, and whole spices until dark and velvety.
7. Prepare the tangy Khatta by simmering soaked tamarind pulp or amchur water with fried chickpea flour dumplings (boondi), jaggery, and crackled mustard seeds.
8. Cook fragrant long-grain basmati rice and sweet Mitha Bhaat (rice simmered with sugar, saffron, raisins, and ghee); serve the feast sequentially onto leaf pattals in traditional pangat order.

stages.title: Origin
stages.headline: Birth of Chana Madra in Chamba & Kangra Valley Kitchens
details: Origin in the Himachal hills: Chana Madra is the undisputed jewel of Himachali festive cooking, originating in the royal state of Chamba and perfected across the Kangra valley as the centerpiece of ceremonial Dham feasts.

Sattvic culinary ethos: Prepared without onion or garlic, Madra relies entirely on the complex transformation of thick whole-milk curd (dahi), pure desi cow ghee, and warming dry spices to achieve its luxurious gravy.

The art of curd stabilization: Hereditary cooks (Botis) developed the patient technique of slow-whisking curd over medium heat until the whey evaporates, the curds emulsify into ghee, and a fragrant golden sauce emerges.

Cooking method: Tender boiled white chickpeas (kabuli chana) or red kidney beans (rajma) are braised slowly in the stabilized spiced yoghurt gravy inside heavy tin-lined brass vessels over wood-fire embers.

stages.title: Recipe
stages.headline: Chana Madra Recipe: 10 Key Ingredients, 8 Steps
details: Key ingredients: kabuli chickpeas (white chana), thick whole-milk curd (dahi), pure desi cow ghee, green cardamom and black cardamom, cinnamon stick (dalchini), cloves and bay leaves, dry ginger powder (saunth), fennel seed powder (saunf), turmeric powder and asafoetida (hing), rock salt (sendha namak).
1. Rinse and soak 1 cup of Kabuli chickpeas in plenty of water overnight for 8 to 10 hours; drain thoroughly.

2. Pressure-cook the soaked chickpeas in 3 cups of water with black cardamom, a cinnamon stick, and 1/2 teaspoon of salt for 4 to 5 whistles until completely soft but retaining their shape; drain and reserve stock.
3. In a bowl, vigorously whisk 2 cups of thick fresh curd until completely silky, smooth, and free of lumps.
4. Heat 3 tablespoons of pure desi cow ghee in a heavy-bottomed brass pot or kadhai over medium flame.
5. Add green cardamom pods, cloves, cinnamon, bay leaf, and a generous pinch of asafoetida (hing), sauteing for 30 seconds until crackling and fragrant.
6. Lower the heat to low, add turmeric powder and dry ginger powder (saunth), then immediately pour in the whisked curd while stirring briskly and continuously in one direction.

7. Cook the curd mixture patiently on medium-low heat for 12 to 15 minutes, stirring without interruption, until the moisture evaporates, the curd turns rich and glossy, and golden ghee separates at the edges.

8. Add the boiled chickpeas, fennel powder, and rock salt; simmer gently on low flame for 10 to 12 minutes until the chickpeas absorb the rich spiced yoghurt gravy, serving hot with steamed basmati rice.

stages.title: Origin
stages.headline: Birth of Dhuska in Jharkhand & Chota Nagpur Heartlands
stages.narrative: Dhuska originated in the tribal and rural agrarian settlements of Jharkhand across the Chota Nagpur plateau, developed by indigenous communities including the Oraon, Munda, and Santhal as a nutrient-dense, high-energy harvest food. Born from the agrarian rhythm of paddy cultivation and pulse farming, it was created by wet-grinding locally harvested short-grain rice with chana dal (split Bengal gram) and urad dal into a thick batter without chemical leavening, then deep-frying ladlefuls in cold-pressed mustard oil over open wood hearths. Traditionally prepared during major agricultural and social festivals such as Sarhul, Karma, Sohrai, and Teej, as well as community gatherings, Dhuska carries deep cultural significance as an emblem of rural hospitality, eaten hot with earthen-cooked aloo chana sabzi or spicy ghugni.
details: Origin in Jharkhand: Originated in the tribal and agrarian settlements of the Chota Nagpur plateau as a wholesome, sustaining staple for farming communities.
Cultural & festival heritage: Prepared during indigenous harvest celebrations including Sarhul, Karma, and Sohrai to honor forest spirits and agricultural abundance.
Historical documentation: Preserved across centuries through indigenous oral culinary traditions and regional gastronomic chronicles of tribal Jharkhand.
Foundational technique: Batter formed from unfermented wet-ground native rice, chana dal, and urad dal, fried directly in smoking mustard oil to puff like a crisp savoury cake.

stages.title: Recipe
stages.photoLabel: Recipe (Jharkhandi Dhuska Recipe: 10 Key Ingredients, 8 Steps)
stages.headline: Jharkhandi Dhuska Recipe: 10 Key Ingredients, 8 Steps
stages.narrative:
Key ingredients: raw rice (arwa chawal), chana dal (split Bengal gram), urad dal (split black gram), fresh ginger, green chillies, cumin seeds (jeera), carom seeds (ajwain), turmeric powder, asafoetida (hing), mustard oil for deep frying.

1. Rinse raw rice, chana dal, and urad dal in cold water, then soak them together in ample water for at least 5 to 6 hours or overnight.
2. Drain the soaking water and transfer the softened grains to a wet grinder or mixer jar along with chopped ginger and green chillies.
3. Grind with small splashes of water into a thick, smooth, and cohesive batter resembling the consistency of pancake or idli batter.
4. Transfer the batter to a deep bowl, then vigorously whisk by hand in one direction for 3 to 4 minutes to incorporate air for natural puffing.
5. Add cumin seeds, ajwain, turmeric powder, a generous pinch of asafoetida, and salt to taste; fold gently into the batter.
6. Heat mustard oil in a heavy cast-iron kadhai over medium-high flame until it smokes lightly, then lower heat slightly to stabilize temperature.
7. Pour a ladleful of batter directly into the center of the hot oil in a steady stream without spreading; gently spoon hot oil over the top until it puffs up like a balloon.
8. Flip carefully and fry until both sides turn crisp and deep golden-brown; drain on absorbent paper and serve piping hot with spicy Jharkhandi aloo-chana sabzi.

stages.title: Origin
stages.headline: Birth of Chilka Roti in Jharkhand & Tribal Antiquity
stages.narrative: Chilka Roti is an ancient indigenous flatbread native to the Santhal, Munda, Ho, and Oraon tribal communities of Jharkhand. Rooted in the prehistoric agricultural traditions of the Chota Nagpur forested plateau, it was created by rural households to transform freshly harvested unpolished indigenous red rice (arwa chawal) and home-grown chana dal into a nourishing, easily digestible daily bread without yeast or chemical leavening. The name 'Chilka' denotes the delicate, peel-like thinness of the crepe-like flatbread as it lifts off the griddle. Deeply tied to the seasonal rhythm of the Kharif rice harvest and forest ceremonies like Sarhul, Chilka Roti was traditionally poured onto earthen or cast-iron tawas swabbed with oil using fresh sal leaf twigs, embodying tribal resourcefulness and revered culinary minimalism.
details: Origin in Jharkhand: Developed by Santhal, Munda, Ho, and Oraon communities across the Chota Nagpur plateau as an ancestral unfermented grain flatbread.
Cultural & forest roots: Prepared during Kharif harvest celebrations and Sarhul forest festivals, honoring village deities with the year's first milled rice.
Historical documentation: Preserved across generations through tribal oral history, community feasts, and indigenous ethno-botanical culinary records of Jharkhand.
Core identity: Batter of unpolished native red rice and split Bengal gram, poured onto hot griddles oiled with sal leaf twigs to produce paper-thin, soft rotis.

stages.photoLabel: Recipe (Jharkhandi Chilka Roti Recipe: 10 Key Ingredients, 8 Steps)
stages.headline: Jharkhandi Chilka Roti Recipe: 10 Key Ingredients, 8 Steps
stages.narrative:
Key ingredients: raw unpolished rice (arwa chawal), chana dal (split Bengal gram), fresh ginger, cumin seeds (jeera), green chillies, water, rock salt, pure mustard oil (for tawa greasing), fresh coriander leaves, sal leaf or banana leaf (for traditional resting).

1. Measure raw rice and chana dal in a 2:1 ratio, wash thoroughly in cold water, and soak together for 5 to 6 hours or overnight.
2. Drain the soaked grains and place them in a stone sil-batta or wet mixer jar along with chopped ginger and green chillies.
3. Grind with measured additions of water until transformed into a silky, runny, and lump-free batter with a thin pouring consistency.
4. Pour the batter into a large bowl; season with salt, crushed cumin seeds, and finely chopped coriander leaves, stirring thoroughly.
5. Heat a seasoned cast-iron tawa over medium flame and grease the surface lightly with mustard oil using a folded cloth or brush.
6. Stir the batter well from the bottom, then pour a generous ladleful onto the center of the hot tawa.
7. Immediately swirl the griddle or lightly glide the back of the ladle in circular outward motion to form a thin, even disc.
8. Drizzle a few drops of mustard oil along the perimeter; cook until the edges release freely, flip to lightly freckle the reverse side, fold into quarters, and serve hot with chana dal jhor.

stages.headline: Birth of Masala Dosa in Karnataka & the South
stages.narrative: The dosa has ancient beginnings in South India and Karnataka. A preparation named 'dosaka' is first documented in the 12th-century Sanskrit work Manasollasa, compiled by King Someshvara III of the Western Chalukya dynasty ruling northern Karnataka. In early times, dosas were thick, soft griddle-cakes cooked on clay plates using fermented black gram and rice batter. The dish evolved deeply within the temple kitchens of Udupi and Old Mysore, where natural overnight fermentation was perfected into an art.

Temple heritage: Perfected in Udupi Madhwa temple kitchens through stone-ground wild fermentation of rice and black gram.
Cooking method: Naturally aerated batter swirled on griddles over wood hearths into soft, wholesome breakfast cakes.

stages.headline: Masala Dosa Recipe: 8 Steps
stages.narrative:
Sona Masuri rice, urad dal, fenugreek seeds, poha, potatoes, onions, green chillies, mustard seeds, curry leaves, pure desi ghee or butter.

1. Soak Sona Masuri rice, urad dal, fenugreek seeds, and poha in water for 5 hours, then grind in a wet grinder to a silky, aerated batter.
2. Add salt, mix thoroughly with hands to introduce natural microflora, and ferment overnight in a warm spot for 8 to 12 hours.
3. Boil potatoes until tender, peel, and coarsely hand-mash into uneven chunks.
4. Heat oil in a pan, crackle mustard seeds, cumin, chana dal, urad dal, and curry leaves; saute sliced onions, green chillies, and ginger until translucent.
5. Stir in turmeric, salt, mashed potatoes, and a splash of water; simmer the potato palya for 3 minutes and finish with fresh coriander.
6. Heat a seasoned cast-iron tawa over medium-high heat, sprinkle water to test sizzle, and wipe with a lightly oiled cloth.
7. Pour a ladleful of fermented batter in the centre and swirl smoothly in outward circular motions into a thin, even crepe.
8. Drizzle pure ghee or butter along the edges, cook until golden crisp, spread red chutney inside, add warm potato palya, fold neatly, and serve hot with coconut chutney and sambar.

stages.title: Origin
stages.headline: Birth of Bisi Bele Bath in Karnataka & the Mysore Palace
stages.narrative: Bisi Bele Bath originates from the royal kitchens of the Mysore Palace under the Wodeyar dynasty in southern Karnataka. The name translates in Kannada to 'hot lentil rice' (bisi = hot, bele = lentil, bath = rice preparation). Palace cooks formulated it as an elaborate, wholesome royal offering to the palace deities, combining short-grain rice with toor dal, wild forest spices, aged tamarind, and desi ghee. From the Mysore court, the dish was embraced by Karnataka's temple traditions and Madhwa community kitchens, establishing its iconic status across the state.

Name and heritage: Named from Kannada 'Bisi' (hot), 'Bele' (lentil/dal), and 'Bath' (seasoned rice dish).
Distinctive spice identity: Characterised by bisi bele bath podi featuring native Karnataka Byadagi chillies and wild kapok buds (marathi moggu).
Cooking method: Slow simmered in heavy brass cauldrons until rice, lentils, tamarind, and spices coalesce into a rich, unified porridge.

stages.headline: Bisi Bele Bath Recipe: 8 Steps
stages.narrative:
Sona Masuri rice, toor dal, mixed vegetables (carrots, beans, peas), tamarind extract, jaggery, Byadagi dry red chillies, kapok buds (marathi moggu), dry coconut (copra), cashew nuts, pure desi ghee.

1. Rinse Sona Masuri rice and toor dal together, then pressure-cook with water and a pinch of turmeric for 4 to 5 whistles until soft and easily mashable.
2. Dry-roast Byadagi chillies, chana dal, urad dal, coriander seeds, cumin, fenugreek, marathi moggu, and cinnamon until aromatic; add grated copra and hing, cool, and grind into a fine bisi bele bath spice powder.
3. Boil chopped carrots, French beans, potatoes, peas, and shallots in water with salt until tender.
4. Add thick tamarind extract, grated jaggery, and 3 tablespoons of the prepared spice powder to the cooked vegetables and simmer for 5 minutes.
5. Lightly mash the cooked rice and dal, then combine them into the bubbling spiced vegetable broth.
6. Adjust consistency with warm water to a smooth, pourable porridge and simmer on low heat for 7 minutes, stirring gently to prevent sticking.
7. Heat pure desi ghee in a pan, crackle mustard seeds and curry leaves, and fry cashew nuts and broken dried chillies until golden.
8. Pour the sizzling ghee tempering over the bisi bele bath, mix well, rest for 2 minutes, and serve piping hot topped with crisp kara boondi.

stages.title: Origin
stages.photoLabel: Appam with Vegetable Stew - Origin (Birth of the food)
stages.headline: Birth of Appam with Vegetable Stew in Kerala
stages.narrative: Appam is a lacy, fermented rice-and-coconut pancake of Kerala. It is also eaten in Tamil Nadu and in Sri Lanka, where it is called a hopper. Food historian K. T. Achaya is cited as saying appam appears in ancient Tamil Sangam literature, with poems describing appams sold in the markets of ancient Madurai. No date is given in the source. Another view, from food researcher Dr Tanya Abraham, is that an early form may have come to Kerala with Kochi's Jewish community, whose dish Oppo is "believed to have gradually evolved" into appam. Cochin Jews are also said to have used fresh toddy instead of yeast to ferment it. The name may come from the Sanskrit "apupa" (a fried dainty). This is uncertain. Appam is traditionally cooked in an appachatti, a deep wok-shaped pan. The vegetable stew is a mild coconut-milk stew served with appam, and the pairing is often served at festive meals such as Christmas and Easter in Kerala. The origin of the stew itself is not documented in the sources. No single origin, date or creator is documented with certainty. Appam seems to have more than one origin, shaped by several communities over centuries.

stages.headline: Appam with Vegetable Stew Recipe: 8 Steps
stages.narrative:
raw rice, cooked rice, coconut milk (thin and thick), yeast, sugar, salt, mixed vegetables (potato, carrot, beans, peas), onion, green chilli and ginger, whole spices (cloves, peppercorns, cinnamon, cardamom) with curry leaves and coconut oil.

1. Soak the rice. Rinse the raw rice and soak it for 4 to 5 hours, then drain. (The grains should look swollen.)
2. Grind the batter. Grind the soaked rice with a little cooked rice and water. (The batter should be smooth, with no gritty grains.)
3. Ferment the batter. Mix yeast and sugar in warm water, stir it in with some coconut milk, cover and leave overnight, about 8 to 10 hours. (It is ready when the batter has risen and is bubbly. Keep it warm in cold weather.)
4. Start the stew. Heat coconut oil, fry the whole spices, then add onion, green chilli, ginger and curry leaves. (The onion should turn soft and see-through, and the spices should smell fragrant.)
5. Cook the vegetables. Add the mixed vegetables, fry for about 2 minutes, then pour in the thin coconut milk and simmer. (The vegetables are done when they are tender but still hold their shape.)
6. Finish the stew. Stir in the thick coconut milk, adjust the salt and warm it gently. Do not boil. (The stew should look creamy and not split.)
7. Cook the appam. Add salt to the batter. Heat the appam pan, pour in a ladle of batter, swirl it, cover and cook on low heat without flipping. (The centre should be soft and thick, and the edges thin, lacy and golden.)
8. Serve. Serve the hot appam with the warm stew, garnished with curry leaves and a drizzle of coconut oil. (Serve right away while the appam is soft.)

stages.headline: Birth of Fish Molee in Kerala
stages.narrative: Fish molee (also spelled moilee, and called meen moilee in Malayalam) is a mild, creamy Kerala fish curry cooked in coconut milk with green chillies, ginger, garlic and curry leaves. It is said to have originated in central Kerala. Its cooking is linked to Portuguese influence on Kerala's coast. Some sources say the recipe dates to the 15th century, but this is a legend and is not documented history. A popular legend says traditional Kerala fish curries were too hot for Portuguese officials, so a woman named Molly cooked it with coconut milk and mild green chillies instead of red chillies, and the dish became known as "fish molee". This is a folk story, not a proven origin of the name. The sources do not explain the name's etymology any further, and no date, creator or exact place is documented with certainty.

stages.headline: Fish Molee Recipe: 8 Steps
stages.narrative:
seer fish (or pomfret), coconut milk (thin and thick), coconut oil, green chillies, ginger and garlic, onion, tomato, curry leaves, whole spices (cloves, cardamom, cinnamon), turmeric with black pepper, salt and lime juice.

1. Marinate the fish. Rub the fish with turmeric, black pepper, salt and lime juice and rest it for 30 minutes. (Every piece should be coated evenly.)
2. Fry the fish lightly. Shallow fry the fish in coconut oil for 3 to 4 minutes on each side, then set it aside. (It should be lightly browned, not dark.)
3. Temper the spices. In the same oil, fry the cloves, cardamom, cinnamon, curry leaves and slit green chillies for a few seconds. (They should smell fragrant and the curry leaves should crackle.)
4. Cook the base. Add the onions, ginger and garlic and cook, then stir in the turmeric. (The onions should turn soft and pinkish with no raw smell.)
5. Add the thin coconut milk. Lower the heat, add the thin coconut milk, tomato and a little water, and bring to a gentle simmer. (Small bubbles only. Do not boil hard.)
6. Cook the fish. Return the fish and shake the pan to coat it instead of stirring. Cover and cook for about 10 minutes. (The fish should be opaque and the pieces should stay whole.)
7. Add the thick coconut milk. On low heat, add the thick coconut milk and a little lime juice, and heat until it just simmers. (The gravy should look creamy and not split. Do not overcook.)
8. Serve. Garnish with curry leaves and serve hot with appam or steamed rice. (Serve right away while the gravy is silky.)

3. Temper the spices. In the same oil, fry the cloves, cardamom, cinnamon, curry leaves and slit green chillies for a few seconds. (They should smell fragrant and the curry leaves should crackle.)
4. Cook the base. Add the onions, ginger and garlic and cook, then stir in the turmeric. (The onions should turn soft and pinkish with no raw smell.)
5. Add the thin coconut milk. Lower the heat, add the thin coconut milk, tomato and a little water, and bring to a gentle simmer. (Small bubbles only. Do not boil hard.)
6. Cook the fish. Return the fish and shake the pan to coat it instead of stirring. Cover and cook for about 10 minutes. (The fish should be opaque and the pieces should stay whole.)
7. Add the thick coconut milk. On low heat, add the thick coconut milk and a little lime juice, and heat until it just simmers. (The gravy should look creamy and not split. Do not overcook.)
8. Serve. Garnish with curry leaves and serve hot with appam or steamed rice. (Serve right away while the gravy is silky.)

stages.title: Origin
stages.headline: Birth of Puttu in Kerala and Tamil Traditions
stages.narrative: Puttu is a steamed cylinder of coarsely ground rice flour layered with grated coconut. The name is said to mean "portioned" in Malayalam and Tamil. It is Kerala's best-known breakfast dish, but many historians point to Tamil Nadu as its earliest home, so Kerala cannot claim to be first. The earliest known reference is said to be in the Tamil devotional work Thiruppugazh by Arunagirinathar, dated to the 15th century. The 16th-century Thiruvilaiyadal Puranam tells a legend of Lord Ganesha helping an old woman who sells puttu near a Madurai temple. This is a legend, not evidence of origin. Early Malayalam literature does not mention puttu. This suggests Tamil and Malayalam speakers shared a food culture, and puttu may also have developed in Kerala. This is a suggestion, not proof. A popular claim says Portuguese sailors introduced puttu to Kerala because it was easy to steam. One article argues this is a myth, because puttu was likely cooked in clay, metal or bamboo steamers long before the Portuguese arrived. Puttu was traditionally steamed in bamboo logs. Similar dishes exist elsewhere, such as pittu in Sri Lanka and sunga pitha in Assam. No single date, creator or place of origin is documented with certainty.

stages.title: Recipe
stages.headline: Puttu Recipe: 8 Steps
stages.narrative:
puttu flour (coarse rice flour) or parboiled rice, grated coconut, salt, water.

1. Mix the flour. Put the puttu flour in a wide bowl, add salt and some of the grated coconut, and mix. (The coconut should be spread evenly through the flour.)
2. Moisten the flour. Sprinkle in water a little at a time and mix gently with your fingers. (A pressed handful should hold as a lump, then crumble when pressed again.)
3. No puttu flour? Make it from rice. Soak parboiled rice for 4 hours, drain it, and dry it on a cloth for 30 minutes. Grind it to a powder, sieve it, and grind the coarse leftovers again. Mix in salt and coconut, then moisten it as in step 2. (The flour should feel coarse and sandy, not like a fine powder.)
4. Heat the steamer. Boil water in the bottom vessel of the puttu steamer. (The water should be boiling before you add the cylinder.)
5. Layer the puttu. In the puttu cylinder, add a spoon of coconut, then the flour mixture up to halfway, then another spoon of coconut. Repeat once more until the cylinder is full. (Do not pack the flour down. Keep it loose.)
6. Steam the puttu. Cover with the lid and steam for about 10 minutes. (Steam should come out of the vent at the top.)
7. Unmould the puttu. Let it cool for 3 to 4 minutes, then push it out with the skewer. (It should come out as a whole cylinder that crumbles softly.)
8. Serve. Serve hot, traditionally with kadala (black chickpea) curry, bananas or pappadam. (Serve while the puttu is still warm and soft.)

stages.title: Origin
stages.headline: Indori Poha: Origin & Street Food Heritage
stages.narrative:
Indori poha is a famous breakfast and street food of Indore, in Madhya Pradesh. Poha is the Hindi name for flattened rice. "Indori" means "of Indore". Poha is a widely eaten Indian food. What makes this version Indori is how it is cooked and topped. Unlike many other poha styles, it is steamed instead of being cooked directly with other ingredients, and the onions are not sauteed. Chopped raw onions go on top. It is finished with toppings such as sev, masala boondi (nukti), pomegranate and jeeravan masala, and is often served with hot jalebi. No reliable historical record gives the exact year, place or creator of Indori poha. One popular account says rulers from Maharashtra brought poha to this region, but this is not documented.

Why it is famous:
- Its own cooking style: the poha is steamed, which gives it a distinct soft texture and taste.
- Balanced flavour: sweet, tangy and spicy together, with fennel seeds adding a light sweetness.
- Many textures in one plate: soft poha, crunchy sev and boondi, fresh onion and juicy pomegranate.
- Jeeravan masala: a spice blend from Madhya Pradesh whose taste is different from chaat masala or garam masala.
- Poha-jalebi: hot, sweet jalebi with savoury poha is the classic Indore pairing.
- Morning street food: vendors across Indore sell it in the morning, often next to kachori and samosa.
- Wide reach: it is also sold in nearby cities such as Ujjain, Dewas, Ratlam and Bhopal, and is becoming popular in other states.

stages.title: Recipe
stages.headline: Indori Poha Recipe: 10 Steps
stages.narrative:
Thick or medium-thick poha (flattened rice), Turmeric, sugar and salt, Oil, Mustard seeds and fennel seeds, Green chilli, Onion (raw, chopped), Fresh coriander leaves, Jeeravan masala, Ratlami or Indori sev, and masala boondi (nukti), Lemon, Pomegranate (optional), Hot jalebi (for serving, optional).

1. Rinse the poha. - Rinse thick poha in a strainer under clean running water. Do not over-rinse, or it turns mushy.
2. Drain and rest. - Drain well. The flakes should be soft but whole. If still firm, sprinkle a little water and wait a few minutes.
3. Add the dry seasoning. - Add turmeric, sugar and salt to the poha and mix lightly.
4. Make the tempering. - Heat oil on low to medium-low heat. Add mustard seeds, then fennel seeds, then green chilli.
5. Add the poha. - Keep the heat low and mix gently until the colour turns light yellow.
6. Steam the poha. - Cover with a lid and steam on low heat for about 1 to 2 minutes. Stir and switch off the heat.
7. Plate it hot. - Take the hot poha on a plate.
8. Add the fresh toppings. - Top with chopped raw onion and coriander, sprinkle jeeravan masala, and add pomegranate.
9. Add the crunch. - Top with masala boondi (nukti) and Ratlami or Indori sev.
10. Finish and serve. - Squeeze lemon juice on top. Serve straight away, with hot jalebi.

Use thick or medium-thick poha. Steam it; the onions are not sauteed. Recipes differ from vendor to vendor, and some vendors add peas.

stages.title: Origin
stages.headline: Bhutte Ka Kees: Origin & Malwa Heritage
stages.narrative:
Bhutte Ka Kees is a famous street food and traditional delicacy of Madhya Pradesh, especially celebrated across the Malwa region including Indore (famous in Sarafa Bazaar night market and Chappan Dukan). "Bhutta" means corn on the cob, and "Kees" comes from "keesna" (to grate in Hindi). Fresh tender corn kernels are grated fresh, releasing sweet corn pulp and juice, then slow-braised in full-cream milk, tempered with mustard seeds, cumin, hing (asafoetida), and green chillies, and finished with freshly grated coconut, coriander, and lemon juice. No reliable historical record gives the exact year, place or creator of Bhutte Ka Kees, though local tradition associates it with Holkar-era royal banquets and Malwa monsoon harvest feasts.

Why it is famous:
- Its own cooking style: fresh corn is grated to extract juices and slow-braised in milk, yielding a luscious creamy and grainy texture.
- Balanced flavour: natural corn sweetness harmonized with spicy green chillies, aromatic hing, and tangy fresh lemon.
- Night street food royalty: an iconic attraction at Indore's legendary Sarafa Bazaar and Chappan Dukan.
- Seasonal harvest celebration: traditionally crafted during monsoons when tender desi bhutta is harvested in Malwa.
- Rich garnishes: served steaming hot topped with freshly grated coconut, coriander, crunchy sev, and a dash of jeeravan masala.
- Wide reach: popular across Indore, Ujjain, Ratlam, Bhopal, and now featured on menus nationwide.

stages.title: Recipe
stages.headline: Recipe: 10 Preparation Steps
stages.narrative:
Fresh tender sweet corn (bhutta, grated), Full cream milk, Desi ghee or oil, Mustard seeds and cumin seeds (jeera), Asafoetida (hing), Green chillies (finely chopped), Fresh ginger (grated), Turmeric powder, Sugar and salt, Fresh coconut (scraped/grated), Fresh coriander leaves, Lemon (for tang) and jeeravan masala / sev (optional).

1. Grate the corn. - Husk fresh tender corn cobs and grate using a medium grater to collect pulp and juices.
2. Heat the fat. - Heat ghee or oil in a heavy kadhai over medium-low heat.
3. Splutter the spices. - Add mustard seeds and cumin seeds; once they crackle, add asafoetida (hing).
4. Sauté the aromatics. - Add finely chopped green chillies and grated ginger; sauté for 30 seconds until aromatic.
5. Cook the corn pulp. - Add grated corn, turmeric powder, salt, and a pinch of sugar; sauté on low heat for 3-4 minutes.
6. Pour the milk. - Slowly pour in full cream milk while stirring continuously to blend evenly.
7. Simmer and thicken. - Cover with a lid and cook on low heat for 8-10 minutes, stirring occasionally, until milk is absorbed and corn is tender.
8. Stir in fresh garnish. - Turn off the heat and stir in half of the freshly grated coconut and chopped coriander leaves.
9. Season to taste. - Squeeze fresh lemon juice and dust with jeeravan masala for signature Indori tang.
10. Finish and serve. - Spoon hot into bowls, garnish with remaining grated coconut, coriander, and crispy sev.

Use fresh tender corn. Grating rather than blending retains the quintessential texture. Add milk gradually on low heat to achieve creamy consistency.
