stages.title: Origin
stages.headline: Dal Bafla: Origin & Festive Malwa Heritage
stages.narrative:
Dal Bafla is the signature celebratory feast of Madhya Pradesh, celebrated throughout the Malwa and Bundelkhand regions (notably in Ujjain, Indore, Ratlam, and Maheshwar). It is related to Rajasthani baati but distinguished by its unique two-stage cooking: dough balls of coarse whole-wheat flour, semolina, and ghee are boiled in spiced water first, then roasted over cow-dung embers or baked in an oven until blistered and golden. The boiling gelatinizes the starch, ensuring the inside remains incredibly tender and fluffy, while the baking creates a crisp outer crust. Hot baflas are cracked open, drenched completely in melted desi ghee, and paired with spicy five-lentil Panchmel Dal, fiery garlic chutney, and sweet churma.

Why it is famous:
- Unique boil-then-bake method: boiling before baking ensures a soft, tender crumb unlike the firmer, dry Rajasthani baati.
- Desi ghee immersion: hot baflas are cracked open and fully bathed in warm desi ghee, soaking up rich aroma.
- Panchmel Dal accompaniment: served with a harmonious blend of five pulses (toor, moong, chana, urad, masoor) tempered with hing and cumin.
- Sacred banquet centerpiece: standard community meal at weddings, festivals, and pilgrimage feasts across Malwa and the Narmada valley.
- Complex accompaniments: traditionally paired with fiery raw garlic chutney, sweet churma or laddu, and tangy kadhi.
- Wide cultural reverence: celebrated in thali restaurants and royal heritage banquets across Central India.

stages.title: Recipe
stages.headline: Recipe: 10 Preparation Steps
stages.narrative:
Coarse whole-wheat flour (atta), Semolina (sooji / rava), Pure desi ghee, Ajwain (carom seeds), Turmeric powder and pinch of baking soda, Panchmel dal (toor, chana, moong, urad, masoor), Tomatoes and green chillies, Fresh ginger (grated), Cumin seeds and mustard seeds, Asafoetida (hing), Fresh coriander leaves, Spicy red garlic chutney & lemon wedges.

1. Make the dough. - Mix coarse wheat flour, sooji, ajwain, turmeric, salt, and melted ghee (moyen). Rub until crumbly, then knead into a stiff dough with warm water.
2. Shape the baflas. - Divide dough into smooth, medium round balls and make a slight dimple in the center with your thumb.
3. Boil water. - In a large pot, bring water to a rolling boil with 1/2 tsp turmeric and salt.
4. Boil the baflas. - Gently lower the dough balls into boiling water and cook for 12-15 minutes until they float to the surface.
5. Drain and dry. - Lift baflas out with a slotted spoon and dry on a clean towel for 5-10 minutes.
6. Bake until crisp. - Bake in a preheated baati oven or conventional oven at 200°C (390°F) for 20-25 minutes, turning until golden and blistered.
7. Cook the dal. - Pressure cook mixed five lentils with turmeric and salt until soft and creamy.
8. Temper the dal. - Heat ghee in a pan, crackle cumin and mustard seeds, add hing, green chillies, ginger, tomatoes, and spices; pour into dal.
9. Crush and ghee-soak. - Gently crush the hot baked baflas in a napkin and immerse them completely in a bowl of warm desi ghee.
10. Assemble and serve. - Serve piping hot ghee-drenched baflas with Panchmel dal, fiery garlic chutney, sliced onions, and lemon.

Boiling before baking is mandatory for authentic bafla texture. Submerge baflas in ghee while piping hot for complete absorption.

stages.title: Origin
stages.headline: Birth of Vada Pav in Mumbai, Maharashtra
stages.narrative:
Before the 1960s, Vada Pav did not exist, because its two core parts belonged to different worlds. Potatoes had only recently been popularized by the British. The Portuguese pav (bread) was largely shunned by mainstream society because of religious taboos around European baking and the use of wild palm toddy for yeast fermentation. Forced together in a 19th-century wood-fired kitchen, the result would have been very different: dense, sour bread, a roughly hand-mashed potato filling, and frying over smoky wood fires in heavy iron pots of cold-pressed groundnut oil. The two were eaten separately, only in private domestic or colonial settings, before Mumbai's street food culture was born.

Vada Pav is credited to Ashok Vaidya. In 1966, outside Dadar railway station, he combined the potato dumpling (batata vada) and the bread roll into a cheap, quick meal for Mumbai's booming working class. Mill workers rushing to their shifts needed something hot, filling and portable. He split a commercial yeast pav (now socially accepted), smeared it with fiery chutneys, including the signature dry red garlic powder, and stuffed it with a fresh batata vada.

stages.title: Recipe
stages.headline: Mumbai Vada Pav Recipe: 7 Steps
stages.narrative:
potatoes, pav (bread rolls), gram flour (besan), garlic, green chillies. Also needed: oil, salt and red chilli powder.

1. Boil the potatoes, then peel and mash them roughly. (Sign: a knife goes in easily.)
2. Make the filling: fry chopped garlic and green chillies in a little oil, add the mashed potatoes and salt, and mix well. (Sign: it smells fragrant and is dry enough to shape. Let it cool a little.)
3. Shape the filling into round, slightly flat balls. (Sign: they hold their shape without cracking.)
4. Make the batter: whisk gram flour with water and a pinch of salt. (Sign: thick and smooth, with no lumps, and it coats the back of a spoon.)
5. Dip each ball in the batter and fry it in hot oil on medium heat, turning it once or twice. (Sign: golden brown and crisp all over. Drain on paper.)
6. Make the dry garlic chutney: crush garlic with salt and red chilli powder into a coarse powder. (Sign: it looks red and crumbly and smells strong.)
7. Slit the pav without cutting it fully, spread the chutney inside, place the hot vada and press lightly. (Sign: the vada sits snugly. For a modern twist, toast the pav on a griddle with butter first. Serve hot.)

stages.title: Origin
stages.headline: Birth of Puran Poli in Maharashtra
stages.narrative: Puran Poli is a sweet flatbread: a puran (filling) of chana dal and jaggery stuffed into a wheat or maida cover. In the 19th century it was a labor-intensive royal delicacy and a sacred festive offering, prepared only on occasions like Holi and Gudi Padwa. Every step was a test of patience and muscle, because there were no mechanical grinders. It was served hot on fresh banana leaves, mainly to deities and upper-class households. The exact date and creator of Puran Poli are not documented with certainty. The earliest form described here is this 19th-century royal and ritual one.

stages.headline: Puran Poli Recipe: 8 Steps
stages.narrative:
wheat flour, chana dal, jaggery, ghee, cardamom powder, nutmeg powder. Also needed: salt and oil.

1. Wash and boil the chana dal until soft but not mushy. (Sign: a grain mashes easily between two fingers.)
2. Drain the dal and cook it with jaggery on low heat, stirring often. (Sign: it thickens, leaves the sides of the pan and holds its shape on a spoon.)
3. Mash it smooth and mix in cardamom and nutmeg. (Use a puran yantra, food mill or mixer-grinder. Sign: no lumps. Cool it fully, then roll it into smooth balls.)
4. Make the dough: knead flour with water, a little oil and salt, and rest it. (Sign: soft and stretchy, and it springs back when pressed.)
5. Flatten a dough ball, place a puran ball in the centre, bring the edges together and seal. (Sign: no filling is showing.)
6. Dust lightly with flour and roll gently into a round. (Sign: even thickness, no tears, and the filling spread to the edges.)
7. Roast on a hot tawa on medium heat, flipping once, and brush with ghee. (Sign: light brown spots on both sides.)
8. Serve hot with a little ghee on top. (Sign: soft, with the sweet filling visible at the edge.)

stages.title: Origin
stages.headline: Birth of Eromba in Manipur & Meitei Valley Antiquity
stages.narrative: Eromba is a foundational culinary pillar of the Meitei community inhabiting the Imphal Valley of Manipur, tracing its origins to ancient antiquity. Etymologically derived from the Meitei expression 'eeru taana lonba' (meaning mixing and stirring something watery), the dish developed as an ingenious response to the ecological landscape of the valley, bordered by mist-covered hills and rich wetland ecosystems like Loktak Lake. To ensure year-round preservation of aquatic proteins during monsoons and dry spells, the Meitei perfected 'Ngari'—sun-dried freshwater fish (Puntius sophore) fermented without salt in mustard-oil-glazed earthen urns (ngari chaphu). In Eromba, roasted ngari is hand-mashed with boiled native potatoes, seasonal tree beans (yongchak), bamboo shoots, and fiercely pungent Umorok (king chilli), creating a soul-stirring comfort dish eaten daily with steamed aromatic rice.
details: Origin in Manipur: Rooted in the ancient agrarian and lacustrine civilization of the Meitei people in the fertile Imphal Valley.
Cultural & communal significance: Central to Meitei everyday dining and seasonal celebrations; arrival of winter yongchak (tree beans) triggers community feasts.
Historical documentation: Codified in Meitei oral culinary tradition and regional historical accounts documenting ancient fish fermentation in ngari chaphu urns.
Culinary philosophy: Zero-oil preparation blending fermented umami, mountain tubers, wetland greens, and volcanic Umorok heat into a coarse hand-mashed emulsion.
stages.evidenceNote: Meitei cultural documentation and regional anthropological studies record ancestral ngari fermentation and vegetable mashing traditions in Manipur.

stages.title: Recipe
stages.photoLabel: Recipe (Manipuri Eromba Recipe: 10 Key Ingredients, 8 Steps)
stages.headline: Manipuri Eromba Recipe: 10 Key Ingredients, 8 Steps
stages.narrative:
Key ingredients: ngari (traditional fermented freshwater fish), medium potatoes, yongchak (tree beans/stink beans) or seasonal beans, fresh umorok (king chilli) or dried red chillies, tender bamboo shoot (soibum), maroi nakupi (Manipuri chives), fresh coriander leaves, spring onions, starchy vegetable broth, rock salt.

1. Peel and quarter the potatoes; scrape the rough outer skin of the yongchak pods and slice them into two-inch pieces.
2. In a deep saucepan, place the potatoes, yongchak, sliced bamboo shoots, and dried red chillies or Umorok with enough water to submerge.
3. Bring to a rolling boil over medium heat and cook uncovered until the vegetables and tubers are completely fork-tender.
4. Meanwhile, gently toast the ngari pieces on a dry tawa or wrapped in a banana leaf over low flame until fragrant and lightly charred.
5. Remove the boiled potatoes and chillies from the saucepan into a wide mashing bowl, reserving the aromatic vegetable cooking liquid.
6. Add the roasted ngari and salt to the bowl; use the back of a spoon or pestle to vigorously crush the chillies and ngari into a spicy paste.
7. Add the boiled potatoes and yongchak pieces into the paste, mashing thoroughly by hand while retaining pleasant coarse rustic chunks.
8. Pour in a few tablespoons of the reserved warm vegetable broth to achieve a thick, cohesive gravy; fold in finely chopped maroi nakupi, spring onions, and coriander, and serve with hot rice.

stages.title: Origin
stages.headline: Birth of Singju in Manipur & Ancient Herbal Traditions
stages.narrative: Singju is an ancient, highly revered spicy botanical salad originating in the Meitei kingdom of Manipur. Etymologically rooted in the Meitei words 'Manaa-Masing' (green vegetables and medicinal herbs) and 'Suba' (combining or mixing together), the contracted name 'Singju' represents centuries of intimate botanical knowledge and foraging culture in the wetland fringes and forested valleys of Manipur. Conceived as both an everyday afternoon refreshment and a vital medicinal digestive, Singju was assembled by thinly julienning seasonal forest produce—such as lotus stem (thambou), cabbage, green papaya, banana inflorescence, and wild herbs like phakpai and lomba—and tossing them raw with roasted perilla seeds (thoiding) or roasted ngari (fermented fish) with fiery chillies. Unlike conventional salads, Singju uses no cooking oil, drawing its rich mouthfeel from the essential polyunsaturated oils released by crushed roasted perilla seeds.
details: Origin in Manipur: Born in the ancient Meitei settlements of Manipur from centuries of seasonal herb gathering and agricultural foraging.
Cultural dualism: Prepared in two distinct ritual forms—vegetarian Thoiding-Besan Singju for religious ceremonies, and Ngari Singju for everyday domestic delight.
Historical documentation: Mentioned in Meitei traditional chronicles and folklore as an indispensable health-giving salad utilizing local medicinal herbs.
Culinary signature: Zero-oil raw preparation bound by hand with ground roasted perilla seeds, roasted gram flour, pounded chillies, and fragrant marsh herbs.

stages.title: Recipe
stages.photoLabel: Recipe (Manipuri Singju Recipe: 10 Key Ingredients, 8 Steps)
stages.headline: Manipuri Singju Recipe: 10 Key Ingredients, 8 Steps
stages.narrative:
Key ingredients: crisp fresh cabbage, tender lotus stems (thambou) or raw papaya, thoiding (perilla seeds), roasted gram flour (besan), roasted ngari (fermented fish) or dry peas, dried red chillies (morok), fresh umorok (king chilli), phakpai (Himalayan knotweed) or coriander, salt, fresh lemon juice.

1. Thoroughly wash the cabbage, lotus stems (or green papaya), and indigenous herbs in ice-cold water and pat completely dry.
2. Using a sharp knife, shred the cabbage into ultra-fine chiffonade strips and slice the lotus stems into paper-thin discs.
3. Dry-roast the perilla seeds (thoiding) in a heavy tawa over low heat until they begin to crackle and release an aromatic, nutty fragrance.
4. Transfer the roasted perilla seeds to a stone mortar and pestle; grind into a coarse, oily, aromatic powder.
5. In the same dry pan, lightly roast the chickpea flour (besan) until golden and fragrant, then set aside to cool.
6. For the seasoning paste, roast the ngari pieces and dry red chillies over low flame, then pound them with a pinch of rock salt into a pungent paste (morok metpa).
7. In a large mixing bowl, combine the shredded cabbage, sliced lotus stems, chopped phakpai, roasted perilla powder, and roasted besan.
8. Add the spicy morok metpa paste and lemon juice; toss and massage vigorously by hand to bruise the greens so they absorb the dressing, and serve immediately.

stages.title: Origin
stages.headline: Birth of Jadoh in the Pine Hills of Meghalaya
stages.narrative: Jadoh is the undisputed ceremonial centerpiece of the indigenous Khasi community in the rolling pine-forested plateau of Meghalaya. The name derives directly from the Khasi words 'Ja' (cooked rice) and 'Doh' (meat). Historically prepared during milestone community gatherings, sacred clan rituals, and harvest festivals like Nongkrem, Jadoh honours the sacred staple grain—indigenous hill red rice—by cooking it directly in rich rendered pork juices. Unlike plains pulaos that emphasize whole dry spices, authentic Khasi cooking relies on the elemental power of fiery mountain ginger, locally grown Lakadong turmeric, pungent onions, and high-fat pork cuts slow-braised together in a heavy iron or aluminium pot.

Etymological identity: Deriving directly from 'Ja' (rice) and 'Doh' (meat), the dish celebrates the sacred union of highland rice and pork sustenance.
Ritual & festival role: Historically prepared during major clan rites, family gatherings, and community festivals like Shad Suk Mynsiem and Nongkrem.
Indigenous flavour philosophy: Relies on minimal aromatics—fresh hill ginger, wild bay leaves, black pepper, and Lakadong turmeric—allowing the pure meat and rice to shine.

stages.title: Recipe
stages.headline: Jadoh Recipe: 10 Key Ingredients, 8 Steps
stages.narrative:
Key ingredients: indigenous Khasi red hill rice (Jaha / Khaw Khasi), fresh pork with fat and skin intact (doh sniang), cold-pressed mustard oil, finely chopped local shallots or onions, freshly crushed ginger root, crushed garlic cloves, freshly cracked black peppercorns, ground turmeric powder (Meghalaya Lakadong turmeric), bay leaves (sla tejpat), fresh pork broth or rich meat stock.

1. Thoroughly wash the indigenous Khasi red rice in cold water until the rinse runs clear, then drain completely in a colander and set aside for 20 minutes.
2. Cut the pork into bite-sized cubes, ensuring each piece contains a balanced layer of skin, succulent fat, and tender meat.
3. Heat mustard oil in a heavy-bottomed iron pot or deep degchi over medium heat until fragrant, then add bay leaves (sla tejpat) and chopped onions.
4. Fry the onions for 4 to 5 minutes until soft and translucent, then add freshly crushed ginger and garlic, sautéing until their raw aroma disappears.
5. Add the pork pieces, Lakadong turmeric powder, cracked black pepper, and salt, stirring vigorously to coat the meat evenly in the aromatics.
6. Sauté the pork on medium flame for 12 to 15 minutes, allowing its natural fats to render out and lightly brown the exterior of the meat.
7. Add the drained red rice into the pot, stirring gently for 2 to 3 minutes so each grain is thoroughly coated in the glistening rendered pork fat and spices.
8. Pour in hot pork broth (in a 1:2 ratio with rice), bring to a rapid boil, then cover with a heavy lid, reduce heat to the lowest setting, and cook for 18 to 20 minutes until the rice is fluffy, tender, and all broth is fully absorbed before resting for 5 minutes.

stages.title: Origin
stages.headline: Birth of Dohneiiong in the Hill Villages of Meghalaya
stages.narrative: Dohneiiong is one of the most distinctive and visually striking meat preparations of the Khasi and Jaintia peoples of Meghalaya. Its name is derived from 'Doh' (meat, specifically pork) and 'Nei-iong' (black sesame seeds). The indigenous black sesame grown in the Meghalaya hills is prized for its high oil content, earthy minerality, and intense nutty fragrance. Khasi homemakers developed the technique of dry-roasting the raw black sesame seeds on hot iron griddles until popping, then grinding them on flat stone querns with a little water into a thick, glossy black paste. Simmered patiently with country pork, the sesame oils emulsify with the melting pork fat to produce an unctuous, pitch-black gravy rich in natural nutrients.
details: Origin in the Khasi Hills: Dohneiiong is an ancestral pork specialty native to the Khasi and Jaintia communities of Meghalaya.
Etymological significance: Named from 'Doh' (meat/pork) and 'Nei-iong' (black sesame seeds), reflecting its two vital culinary pillars.
Unique sesame processing: Indigenous black sesame seeds are gently dry-toasted to unlock deep nutty aromatics and stone-ground into a rich, jet-black paste.
Nutritive cold-climate alchemy: The combination of sesame plant oils and slow-rendered pork fat provided vital calories and heat in misty Himalayan winters.

stages.title: Recipe
stages.headline: Dohneiiong Recipe: 10 Key Ingredients, 8 Steps
stages.narrative:
Key ingredients: fresh pork with fat and skin intact (doh sniang), indigenous black sesame seeds (nei-iong), cold-pressed mustard oil, finely sliced onions, freshly pounded ginger paste, freshly pounded garlic paste, green chillies (slit lengthwise), Lakadong turmeric powder, freshly ground black pepper, warm water (for adjusting gravy consistency).

1. In a dry heavy iron pan over low heat, gently toast the black sesame seeds (nei-iong) for 3 to 4 minutes until they begin to crackle and release a warm, nutty aroma.
2. Transfer the toasted sesame seeds onto a stone quern or small blender, add 3 to 4 tablespoons of warm water, and grind into a thick, smooth, glistening jet-black paste.
3. Cut the pork into bite-sized cubes, ensuring each piece carries a combination of meat, fat, and skin, then rinse and pat dry.
4. Heat mustard oil in a heavy-bottomed pot over medium heat, add the sliced onions and slit green chillies, and sauté for 4 minutes until soft and translucent.
5. Add the pounded ginger paste, garlic paste, Lakadong turmeric powder, and black pepper, stirring continuously for 2 minutes to cook out raw aromatics.
6. Add the pork pieces and rock salt, frying over medium-high heat for 8 to 10 minutes until the exterior of the pork is lightly seared and the fat starts rendering.
7. Stir in the prepared black sesame paste thoroughly, coating every piece of pork until the dish turns dramatically dark and glossy.
8. Pour in one cup of warm water, cover with a tight-fitting lid, reduce heat to low, and simmer gently for 30 to 35 minutes until the pork is meltingly tender and the black sesame gravy is thick, glossy, and clinging to the meat.

4. Heat mustard oil in a heavy-bottomed pot over medium heat, add the sliced onions and slit green chillies, and sauté for 4 minutes until soft and translucent.
5. Add the pounded ginger paste, garlic paste, Lakadong turmeric powder, and black pepper, stirring continuously for 2 minutes to cook out raw aromatics.
6. Add the pork pieces and rock salt, frying over medium-high heat for 8 to 10 minutes until the exterior of the pork is lightly seared and the fat starts rendering.
7. Stir in the prepared black sesame paste thoroughly, coating every piece of pork until the dish turns dramatically dark and glossy.

8. Pour in one cup of warm water, cover with a tight-fitting lid, reduce heat to low, and simmer gently for 30 to 35 minutes until the pork is meltingly tender and the black sesame gravy is thick, glossy, and clinging to the meat.

stages.title: Origin
stages.headline: Birth of Pumaloi in the Hearthside Kitchens of the Khasi Hills
stages.narrative: Pumaloi is one of the oldest and most revered traditional breakfast and festive rice foods of the Khasi people of Meghalaya. Deeply tied to the agricultural cycle of the wet, mist-shrouded Meghalaya hills, it showcases the Khasi mastery of gentle steam cookery without direct boiling. Indigenous varieties of hill rice are washed, sun-dried, and hand-pounded in heavy wooden pestles into a coarse, grainy flour. Rather than kneading into a dense dough, the flour is delicately moistened with drops of salted water until it reaches the consistency of damp breadcrumbs. Cooked in a unique traditional two-tiered terracotta steamer (khiew ranei / khiew pumaloi) over boiling water, the rising vapor cooks the grains into a tender, porous, and fragrant steamed cake.
details: Origin in the Khasi Hills: Pumaloi is an ancient steamed rice staple developed by the Khasi people across the Meghalaya plateau.
Mastery of steam cookery: Perfected to cook native hill rice using gentle steam rather than boiling, preserving the grain's natural aroma and minerals.
The damp-crumb technique: Rather than forming a paste, the flour is rubbed with water droplets into moist crumbs that allow steam to circulate freely.
Two-tier earthen apparatus: Traditionally prepared using a special two-tiered terracotta pot (khiew ranei) with a perforated clay partition over surging boiling water.

stages.title: Recipe
stages.headline: Pumaloi Recipe: 10 Key Ingredients, 8 Steps
stages.narrative:
Key ingredients: indigenous Khasi hill rice (khaw pumaloi / unpolished red or white rice), cold water (for sprinkling and moistening the flour), fine sea salt or rock salt (subtle pinch for dough balance), boiling water (for generating steam in the lower vessel), freshly grated coconut (traditional sweet festive variation), finely grated jaggery (optional layered filling in sweet versions), bamboo mesh or perforated clay disc (siew ranei / internal steam plate), banana leaves (optional liner for the steamer pot), fresh whole milk (accompanying tea or drizzle in morning meals), Tungrymbai or spicy pork curry (traditional savory meal accompaniments).

1. Wash the indigenous Khasi rice thoroughly in cold water, drain, and spread out on a clean cloth to dry completely in the shade for 2 to 3 hours.
2. Grind the dried rice in a heavy mortar or blender into a coarse, sand-like meal (neither too fine like cornstarch nor too coarse like grits).
3. Sieve the flour into a wide mixing bowl, add a light pinch of salt, and mix evenly with your fingertips.
4. Gradually sprinkle cold water a tablespoon at a time over the flour, rubbing and tossing gently with both hands until the flour becomes moist, damp, and crumbly (it should hold its shape when squeezed in your palm, but crumble easily when nudged).
5. Sieve the moist flour through a coarse mesh or colander to break up any large wet clumps and ensure uniform, airy granule distribution.
6. Fill the lower earthen boiling pot (or steamer base) with water and bring it to a vigorous rolling boil to produce a steady stream of steam.
7. Place a perforated clay disc or moistened clean cloth in the upper steamer pot (khiew ranei), loosely spoon in the damp rice flour without pressing or compacting it (optionally layering grated coconut and jaggery in the middle), and level the surface gently.
8. Set the upper pot securely over the boiling base, cover with a tight-fitting clay lid, and steam over medium-high heat for 12 to 15 minutes until fragrant, firm, and fully cooked through before unmoulding onto a warm serving plate.

stages.title: Origin
stages.headline: Birth of Mizo Bai in the Lushai Hills & Forest Foraging Traditions
details: Origin in the Lushai Hills: Bai is the indispensable soul of traditional Mizo daily nutrition, created by indigenous highlanders from fresh seasonal wild greens, bamboo shoots, and garden vegetables.

Zero-oil alkaline philosophy: Unique among global culinary traditions, authentic Bai uses zero cooking oil, relying instead on pure spring water infused with a touch of natural alkaline filtrate (chingal) to soften fibrous greens and retain vibrant colour.
Historical documentation: Rooted in centuries-old Mizo hearth cookery, where every household boiled a fresh pot of Bai twice daily over the kitchen fire to accompany steaming mountain rice.
Cooking method: Fresh mustard greens, tender local beans, and fermented bamboo shoots are boiled together in spring water with pork rind or smoked meat, ginger, and green chillies.

stages.title: Recipe
stages.headline: Mizo Bai Recipe: 10 Key Ingredients, 8 Steps
chips: Pork rind or smoked pork pieces
Natural alkaline extract (chingal) or cooking soda
details: Key ingredients: fresh mustard greens (lai pat), fermented bamboo shoot (rawtuai), pork rind or smoked pork pieces, local green beans or eggplant, natural alkaline extract (chingal) or cooking soda, fresh ginger root, fresh green hill chillies, local aromatic herbs, sea salt, filtered spring water.
1. Wash fresh mustard greens (lai pat) thoroughly in cold water; drain and coarsely chop the leaves and tender stems.
2. Cut local green beans into 2-inch pieces, slice small local eggplants into halves, and prepare fresh fermented bamboo shoots (rawtuai).
3. In a wide pot, bring 3 cups of filtered spring water to a rolling boil over medium-high heat.
4. Add pork rind or smoked pork pieces, crushed fresh ginger root, and slit green chillies, letting them simmer vigorously for 8 minutes to render savoury depth into the broth.
5. Add 1/4 teaspoon of natural alkaline extract (or baking soda) and a level teaspoon of salt into the boiling broth; stir once as it foams gently.
6. Add the sliced eggplants, beans, and fermented bamboo shoots, cooking for 5 minutes until tender-crisp.
7. Drop the chopped mustard greens into the pot, pressing them gently below the bubbling liquid without covering the pot to preserve their bright emerald colour.

8. Simmer on medium flame for 4 to 5 minutes until the greens are tender, remove from heat, let rest for 2 minutes, and ladle hot into traditional wooden or clay bowls to enjoy alongside steamed rice.

details: Origin in community feasts: Sawhchiar is the beloved celebratory one-pot rice and meat congee of Mizoram, prepared during community hunting gatherings (Khuangchawi), festivals (Chapchar Kut), and church fellowships.
Highland comfort heritage: Developed by Mizo highlanders to produce a deeply nourishing, warming, and easily digestible dish from local hill rice and meat slow-simmered over outdoor wood fires.

Historical documentation: Documented in Mizo oral history and colonial records as the supreme communal dish prepared in massive cauldrons for entire villages to celebrate successful hunts and weddings.
Cooking method: Short-grain hill rice and bone-in pork or chicken are simmered together with ginger, garlic, and peppercorns, constantly beaten with a wooden paddle into a rich, creamy porridge.

stages.title: Recipe
stages.headline: Sawhchiar Recipe: 10 Key Ingredients, 8 Steps
chips: Pure lard or drop of mustard oil
details: Key ingredients: indigenous short-grain hill rice, bone-in country pork or chicken, crushed fresh ginger root, garlic cloves, fresh green hill chillies, crushed wild black peppercorns, mustard leaves (for finishing), filtered spring water, pure lard or drop of mustard oil, sea salt.
1. Rinse 1.5 cups of indigenous short-grain rice in cold water and soak for 20 minutes; cut bone-in chicken or pork into bite-sized chunks.
2. In a heavy-bottomed pot, heat 1 teaspoon of lard or oil over medium heat; add crushed fresh ginger root and crushed garlic, sauteing for 1 minute until fragrant.
3. Add the meat pieces and 1 teaspoon of sea salt, searing for 4 to 5 minutes until the meat changes colour and releases its natural juices.
4. Add 6 cups of water and freshly crushed wild black peppercorns; bring to a vigorous rolling boil, skim off any foam from the surface, cover, and simmer for 15 minutes.
5. Drain the soaked rice and add it directly into the boiling meat broth, stirring well to prevent any sticking at the base.
6. Lower heat to medium-low, cover partially, and let simmer for 20 minutes, stirring periodically as the rice grains break down and absorb the flavourful meat stock.
7. Beat the mixture vigorously with a wooden ladle for 2 minutes to break down the starch into a rich, velvety, creamy congee-like porridge.
8. Stir in fresh tender mustard leaves and slit green chillies, simmer for another 2 minutes until wilted, remove from heat, and serve steaming hot in deep bowls.

details: Origin in highland hearth preservation: In the hilly terrain of Mizoram, smoking pork above the open family hearth (rap) was an essential traditional preservation method, transforming fresh cuts into deeply cured, flavourful meat.

The architecture of the 'Rap': Strips of country pork were suspended on bamboo racks directly above the wood-burning cooking fire, allowing the rising smoke of mountain oak and pine to cure the meat over several weeks.
Culinary role: Vawksa Rep is both a cured ingredient and a celebrated finished preparation, cooked simply with fermented bamboo shoots and wild greens to highlight the natural smoke flavour.
Cooking method: Smoked pork slices are boiled in pure spring water with fermented bamboo shoots (rawtuai), crushed mountain ginger, and fresh green chillies without any added cooking oil.

chips: Fresh coriander or local chives (for garnish)
details: Key ingredients: hearth-smoked country pork (vawksa rep), fermented bamboo shoots (rawtuai), fresh ginger root, garlic cloves, fresh green hill chillies, local wild mustard greens, filtered spring water, local aromatic mountain herbs, sea salt, fresh coriander or local chives (for garnish).

2. Place the sliced smoked pork in a pot, cover with 3 cups of water, and bring to a rolling boil over medium-high heat.
3. Boil vigorously for 10 minutes, allowing the tough smoked fibers to soften and render their aromatic smoky fat into the broth.
4. Add crushed fresh ginger root, crushed garlic cloves, and slit green chillies into the bubbling pot.
5. Fold in 1/2 cup of fermented bamboo shoots (rawtuai), stirring gently to combine with the smoked pork and aromatics.
6. Season with sea salt to taste, lower the flame to medium, cover the pot with a lid, and simmer gently for 15 to 20 minutes until the pork is meltingly tender.
7. Add fresh mustard greens or local wild mountain leaves on top, letting them steam and wilt in the fragrant broth for 3 minutes.
8. Remove from heat, garnish with fresh local chives or wild coriander, and serve hot in deep bowls alongside steaming white rice and fresh local chutneys.

details: Origin in ancestral Naga preservation: In the hills of Nagaland, pork cured over family wood-fire kitchen hearths for weeks provided long-lasting sustenance for warriors, hunters, and farming families.

The sacred trinity of Naga cooking: Smoked pork, fermented bamboo shoots (wet bastenga or dry khorisa), and the legendary Naga King Chilli (Bhut Jolokia / Raja Mircha) form the foundational flavor trio of Naga gastronomy.

Historical documentation: Chronicled in anthropological studies of the Angami, Ao, Sema, and Lotha tribes as the quintessential celebratory meat prepared for major festivals such as Moatsu, Sekrenyi, and Tokhu Emong.
Cooking method: Cut into hearty chunks, braised purely in water with fermented bamboo shoots, crushed ginger, garlic, and fresh King Chilli without a single drop of added cooking oil.

stages.headline: Naga Smoked Pork with Bamboo Shoots Recipe: 10 Key Ingredients, 8 Steps
chips: Fermented bamboo shoots (wet bastenga or dry khorisa)

details: Key ingredients: hearth-smoked pork chunks, fermented bamboo shoots (wet bastenga or dry khorisa), fresh naga king chilli (bhut jolokia / raja mircha), fresh ginger root, garlic cloves, sichuan pepper leaves or local wild herbs, local sour tomato (for body), filtered spring water, rock salt, fresh coriander or local chives (for garnish).
1. Clean hearth-smoked pork chunks by scrubbing under warm water; cut into thick 1.5-inch pieces with skin and fat intact.
2. Place the pork chunks in a heavy pot or iron kadhai, add 2.5 cups of filtered spring water, and bring to a rolling boil over medium-high heat.
3. Simmer for 10 to 12 minutes as the smoked pork releases its rich natural fat and infuses the water with deep wood-smoke aroma.
4. Crush fresh ginger root and garlic cloves coarsely in a wooden mortar; add to the boiling pork along with rock salt.
5. Add 1/2 cup of fermented bamboo shoots (bastenga) and 1 small chopped local tomato to balance the rich pork fat.
6. Wearing gloves, lightly pierce or crush half a fresh Naga King Chilli (Raja Mircha) and drop it into the pot, adjusting carefully for heat.
7. Lower the heat to medium-low, cover tightly with a lid, and simmer gently for 25 to 30 minutes until the pork is fork-tender and the gravy thickens to a glossy reduction.
8. Toss in fresh Sichuan pepper leaves or wild local herbs, cook uncovered for 2 minutes, remove from heat, rest for 5 minutes, and serve hot with steamed hill rice.

details: Origin in the Naga highlands: Galho is the traditional savoury one-pot rice and meat porridge of Nagaland, affectionately referred to as the 'Naga Khichdi', developed by agrarian communities to nourish field workers.
The umami power of Axone: Central to authentic Galho is 'Axone' (fermented soybean paste), an indigenous superfood that imparts an earthy, mushroom-like umami depth to the rice and meat.
Seasonal forest greens: Incorporates freshly foraged indigenous mountain greens such as mustard leaves, bitter nightshade leaves, wild coriander, and stinging nettle shoots.

Cooking method: Indigenous hill rice, smoked pork or beef scraps, and axone are simmered together in pure water with ginger, garlic, and fresh birds-eye chillies into a creamy, soul-soothing porridge.

stages.headline: Galho Recipe: 10 Key Ingredients, 8 Steps
chips: Local sour tomato or wild plum
details: Key ingredients: indigenous naga hill rice, hearth-smoked pork or beef cuts, axone (fermented soybean cake), seasonal wild mountain greens (mustard leaves), fresh ginger root, garlic cloves, fresh naga bird's-eye chillies, local sour tomato or wild plum, filtered spring water, rock salt.
1. Rinse 1 cup of indigenous Naga hill rice in cold water and soak for 15 minutes; chop smoked pork or beef into small 1/2-inch bits.
2. In a deep heavy pot, combine the smoked meat scraps with 5 cups of filtered spring water and bring to a vigorous rolling boil over medium-high flame.
3. Add 1 tablespoon of fermented soybean cake (axone), pressing it against the side of the pot with a wooden spoon so it dissolves and disperses completely into the broth.
4. Crush fresh ginger root, garlic cloves, and fresh bird's-eye chillies in a mortar; add to the pot along with rock salt and a chopped sour tomato.
5. Drain the soaked rice and add it into the boiling seasoned broth, stirring well to prevent any grains from catching at the bottom.
6. Lower heat to medium, cover partially, and let simmer for 20 minutes, stirring occasionally as the rice grains soften and expand.
7. Coarsely chop seasonal wild mountain greens (mustard leaves or bitter greens) and stir them into the simmering porridge.
8. Beat gently with a wooden ladle for 2 minutes to create a rich, creamy consistency, simmer for another 3 minutes until greens are tender, remove from heat, and serve piping hot.

stages.title: Origin
stages.headline: Birth of Zutho in Angami Naga Ancient Fermentation Traditions
details: Origin among the Angami Nagas: Zutho is the traditional cloudy, mildly effervescent fermented rice beverage of the Angami Nagas, crafted in villages around Kohima and Dimapur for millennia.

The miracle of 'Piazu': The fermentation relies on an indigenous sprouted-grain starter culture called 'Piazu', prepared by soaking unpolished paddy until sprouted, drying it in the sun, and grinding it into an enzyme-rich malt.

Cultural & community vitality: Central to major agrarian festivals such as Sekrenyi, Zutho is consumed during communal agricultural labor (Mhasie) and shared as an auspicious token of peace and goodwill.
Brewing method: Cooked glutinous rice is cooled, blended with sprouted grain starter (piazu), fermented in clay pots for several days, strained, and diluted with pure spring water.

stages.title: Recipe
stages.headline: Zutho Recipe: 10 Key Ingredients, 8 Steps
details: Key ingredients: indigenous glutinous sticky rice, sprouted unpolished paddy starter (piazu), clean filtered spring water, milled sprouted rice malt, natural wild fermentation yeast enzymes, wild herbal starter plant leaves, fermented rice mash liquor, natural grain brewing sugars, dilution pure spring water, bamboo tumblers (for serving).
1. Thoroughly rinse 2 kg of indigenous glutinous sticky rice in clean spring water and soak for 2 hours.
2. Steam the soaked rice in a traditional perforated wooden or bamboo steamer until fully cooked, soft, and translucent.
3. Spread the hot steamed rice evenly onto clean bamboo mats or wide platters to cool down completely to ambient room temperature (25°C).
4. Prepare the sprouted starter culture (piazu) by finely grinding dried sprouted unpolished paddy into a fragrant, enzyme-rich malt powder.
5. Evenly sprinkle the piazu powder across the cooled rice, tossing gently with clean hands to ensure every grain is inoculated with the natural brewing enzymes.
6. Transfer the inoculated rice into sterilized, pre-warmed terracotta fermentation pots (earthen vats); seal the mouth tightly with banana leaves and clean cloth.
7. Place the pots in a dark, warm corner of the kitchen and let ferment undisturbed for 4 to 6 days until liquid mash forms and a sweet, fruity, mildly alcoholic aroma develops.

8. Strain the fermented rice mash through fine muslin, press gently to extract the milky white liquor, dilute with clean chilled spring water to desired strength, and pour into bamboo tumblers to serve.

stages.title: Origin
stages.headline: Makki di Roti & Sarson da Saag: Agrarian Winter Heritage
stages.narrative:
Makki di roti and sarson da saag is a famous winter staple and comfort food of Punjab. "Makki" means maize or corn, "roti" means flatbread, and "sarson" is the Hindi and Punjabi name for mustard greens. "Saag" refers to cooked leafy greens. It is an agricultural hearth food traditionally cooked during the cold harvest months when fresh mustard leaves are abundant in the fields. The greens are slow-cooked and churned into a thick, coarse mash, while the flatbread is hand-patted from coarse maize flour and griddled on a tawa. It is finished with a generous dollop of freshly churned white butter (makhan) and served with jaggery (gur). No reliable historical record gives the exact year, place or creator of this combination; it has been a rural staple across Punjabi farming households for generations.

Why it is famous:
- Seasonal harmony: fresh winter mustard greens paired with hearty yellow corn flatbread.
- Earthy, robust flavour: mild natural bitterness of mustard greens balanced by sweet jaggery and rich churned butter.
- Traditional churning: slow-cooked greens mashed with a wooden churner (ghotna) produce a distinct rustic texture.
- Gluten-free flatbread technique: hand-patted cornmeal dough griddled until golden and crisp on the edges.
- Classic accompaniment: served with white butter and jaggery, creating a comforting sweet-savoury balance.
- Hearty farm nutrition: traditionally eaten by farmers for energy and warmth through long winter days.
- Wide popularity: a signature emblem of Punjabi hospitality enjoyed across roadside dhabas and homes throughout northern India.

stages.title: Recipe
stages.headline: Makki di Roti & Sarson da Saag Recipe: 10 Steps
stages.narrative:
Fresh mustard greens (sarson), Spinach (palak) and bathua leaves, Maize flour (makki ka atta), Fresh ginger, garlic and green chillies, Onions, Mustard oil or ghee, Salt, Warm water, Fresh white butter (makhan), Jaggery (gur, for serving).

1. Clean and chop the greens. - Wash mustard, spinach and bathua leaves thoroughly in running water to remove grit, then chop them finely.
2. Simmer the greens. - Place the chopped greens in a heavy pot with salt, green chillies, ginger and garlic, and simmer on low heat until tender.
3. Churn the saag. - Mash the softened greens using a traditional wooden churner (ghotna) or hand masher until coarse and thick.
4. Add the maize flour thickener. - Sprinkle a little maize flour into the simmering greens and churn continuously to prevent lumps from forming.
5. Cook the tempering. - Heat ghee or mustard oil in a separate pan. Sauté chopped onions, garlic and ginger until golden brown.
6. Combine and simmer. - Pour the hot tempering into the mashed greens. Stir well and simmer on low heat for a few minutes.
7. Prepare the makki dough. - Mix maize flour with a pinch of salt and gradually add warm water. Knead into a soft, pliable dough.
8. Pat the flatbread. - Divide the dough into balls and pat gently between wet palms or on parchment paper into a round flatbread.
9. Griddle on the tawa. - Transfer carefully to a hot tawa. Cook on medium heat with a little ghee until both sides have golden spots and turn crisp.
10. Finish and serve hot. - Plate the hot makki di roti next to a steaming bowl of sarson da saag. Top with a generous dollop of white butter and serve with jaggery.

Traditional saag combines mustard greens with spinach or bathua to balance bitterness. Always knead maize flour with warm water for easier shaping.

stages.title: Origin
stages.headline: Butter Chicken: Origin & Tandoori Heritage
stages.narrative:
Butter chicken, traditionally known as murgh makhani, is one of the most celebrated dishes of Punjabi and northern Indian cuisine. "Murgh" means chicken, and "makhani" refers to butter, describing a preparation enriched with churned butter and cream. The dish originated from post-partition refugee kitchens where cooks sought a way to revive tandoor-roasted chicken pieces that became dry. Leftover tandoor-charred chicken was gently simmered in a velvety, rich sauce made from ripe tomatoes, butter, cream and gentle spices. The combination of smoky, charred tandoori chicken pieces with a silky, mildly sweet and tangy tomato-butter gravy became an immediate sensation. While popular tradition connects its creation to restaurant kitchens in northern India, exact personal origins remain contested and unverified in official culinary records.

Why it is famous:
- Silky texture: a smooth, strained tomato gravy enriched with fresh butter and dairy cream.
- Smoky char balance: the smokiness of tandoor-roasted chicken cuts cleanly through the creamy gravy.
- Balanced mild spices: aromatic rather than searingly spicy, with green cardamom, Kashmiri chilli and dried fenugreek.
- Kasuri methi finish: crushed dried fenugreek leaves impart a distinct earthy fragrance essential to the dish.
- Global popularity: widely recognized and served in Indian restaurants worldwide as a quintessential comfort dish.
- Tandoor heritage: celebrates the Punjabi tandoor technique of high-heat clay oven roasting.
- Classic pairings: traditionally enjoyed with hot garlic naan, tandoori roti, or fragrant basmati rice.

stages.title: Recipe
stages.headline: Butter Chicken Recipe: 10 Steps
stages.narrative:
Chicken (boneless pieces or bone-in cuts), Hung curd (thick yogurt), Ginger-garlic paste, Kashmiri red chilli powder and turmeric, Ripe tomatoes, Butter and ghee, Fresh dairy cream, Kasuri methi (dried fenugreek leaves), Whole spices (green cardamom, cinnamon, cloves), Salt and a pinch of sugar, Lemon juice.

1. Marinate the chicken. - Coat chicken pieces with curd, ginger-garlic paste, Kashmiri red chilli, lemon juice and salt. Rest for at least 30 minutes.
2. Roast the chicken. - Cook the marinated chicken in a hot tandoor, oven or heavy pan until lightly charred and cooked through. Set aside.
3. Simmer the tomato base. - In a pot, cook chopped ripe tomatoes with whole spices, ginger, garlic and a little water until soft and pulpy.
4. Blend and strain. - Cool the tomato mixture, blend until smooth, and pass through a sieve to achieve a velvety texture.
5. Heat the butter. - Melt butter and a little ghee in a pan on low to medium-low heat. Add a pinch of Kashmiri chilli for colour.
6. Add the strained sauce. - Pour the smooth tomato purée into the butter. Simmer gently until the gravy thickens and oil begins to separate.
7. Add the roasted chicken. - Add the charred chicken pieces to the simmering sauce and mix gently so the meat absorbs the flavours.
8. Season and balance. - Add salt, a pinch of sugar to balance acidity, and gentle garam masala. Simmer on low heat for 5 minutes.
9. Finish with cream and fenugreek. - Stir in fresh dairy cream and crushed kasuri methi between your palms. Switch off the heat.
10. Serve hot. - Garnish with a swirl of fresh cream and a pat of melting butter. Serve with hot tandoori roti or naan.

Straining the tomato puree is key to achieving the signature velvety texture. Kasuri methi should always be crushed lightly before adding.

stages.title: Origin
stages.headline: Amritsari Kulcha: Tandoor Stuffed Bread Heritage
stages.narrative:
Amritsari kulcha is a famous tandoor-baked stuffed flatbread originating from the city of Amritsar, in Punjab. "Kulcha" is a traditional northern Indian leavened or layered flatbread made from refined wheat flour. It is particularly famous around the bustling food lanes and street eateries surrounding the historic center of Amritsar. The dough is laminated with ghee or fat, stuffed with a spicy mixture of mashed potatoes, onions and pomegranate seeds, and baked inside a searing clay tandoor. When pulled crisp and blistering from the tandoor wall, the bread is crushed by hand so the flaky layers shatter, then crowned with fresh white butter. It is traditionally paired with spicy chickpea curry (chole), tangy tamarind-onion chutney (pyaz ki chutney), and pickles. No reliable historical record documents the exact year or creator of the stuffed Amritsari kulcha; it evolved through Punjab's urban tandoor-baking tradition.

Why it is famous:
- Shattering flaky texture: multiple rolled and laminated layers create an irresistible crisp and flaky crust.
- Tandoor char: slapped directly onto the inner clay walls of a high-heat tandoor, giving it blistered spots and a smoky flavour.
- Spicy potato filling: spiced with crushed coriander seeds, anardana (dried pomegranate), carom seeds (ajwain), and green chillies.
- Hand-crushed service: bakers crush the hot bread between their palms before serving to reveal the flaky interior.
- Melting butter crown: generously topped with fresh homemade white butter that melts through the hot shattered layers.
- Iconic breakfast pairing: eaten with spicy Punjabi chole and tangy sliced onion chutney for a filling morning meal.
- Street food pilgrimage: a beloved culinary hallmark that visitors from all over the world seek in Amritsar.

stages.title: Recipe
stages.headline: Amritsari Kulcha Recipe: 10 Steps
stages.narrative:
Refined wheat flour (maida), Boiled and mashed potatoes, Ghee or butter (for lamination and topping), Carom seeds (ajwain) and cumin, Crushed coriander seeds, Dried pomegranate seeds (anardana powder), Green chilli and fresh coriander, Chopped onion, Salt, Water (for kneading), Fresh white butter (for serving).

1. Knead the dough. - Mix refined flour, a pinch of salt and water. Knead into a soft, smooth dough, cover with a damp cloth, and rest for 30 minutes.
2. Laminate the layers. - Roll the dough flat, smear generously with ghee, fold in thirds like an envelope, and repeat to build flaky layers.
3. Prepare the filling. - Mash boiled potatoes with chopped onion, green chilli, fresh coriander, crushed coriander seeds, anardana, ajwain and salt.
4. Portion and stuff. - Divide the layered dough into balls. Flatten each ball slightly, place a generous portion of stuffing in the centre, and seal tightly.
5. Roll and flatten. - Gently pat or roll the stuffed dough with your fingers into a thick round disc, taking care not to tear the edges.
6. Apply moisture and herbs. - Wet the top with a splash of water and press fresh coriander and crushed coriander seeds onto the surface.
7. Bake in tandoor or tawa. - Press the wet side onto the hot inner tandoor wall or an inverted hot iron tawa so it sticks firmly.
8. Crisp both sides. - Cook until the base is firmly set, then invert the tawa directly over the open flame until blisters turn golden brown and crisp.
9. Hand-crush for layers. - Carefully remove the blistering kulcha and crush it gently between your palms to crack the flaky layers open.
10. Butter and serve. - Top immediately with a melting dollop of fresh white butter. Serve piping hot with spicy chole and tamarind onion chutney.

Coarsely crushed coriander seeds and anardana in the stuffing provide the signature Amritsari crunch and tang. Do not use non-stick pans if baking on a tawa.

stages.title: Origin
stages.photoLabel: Dal Baati Churma, Origin (Birth of the food)
stages.headline: Birth of Dal Baati Churma in Mewar, Rajasthan
stages.narrative: Dal baati churma is a Rajasthani trio of baked wheat balls (baati), lentil dal and a sweet crumble (churma). It is traditionally linked to the Mewar kingdom and its founder Bappa Rawal, and to the Guhilot clan, for whom baati is said to have been a wartime meal made from unsalted wheat, ghee and camel milk. A popular story says Rajput soldiers buried dough balls under hot sand before battle and dug out the baked baati on their return. The dal is said to have come later, and churma is said to have started when a cook accidentally poured sugarcane juice on baati, or when women soaked hard baati in jaggery water to keep it soft. These are folk accounts without documentary proof, and no date is given.
details: Origin in Mewar: wheat dough balls baked until hard, then dressed with ghee and eaten with curd or buttermilk.
Traditional cookware: None: dough balls baked in hot sand (believed), later over an open fire.
Traditional heat source: Sun-heated sand (believed); open fire fuelled by wood and dried cow dung.
Cooking method: slow baking in sand or embers, with no dal and no sweet churma at first.
Ingredients known in this epoch: Wheat flour, Ghee, Milk (camel milk in one account), Curd or buttermilk, Sugarcane juice or jaggery (for churma).

stages.title: Recipe
stages.headline: Dal Baati Churma Recipe: 8 Steps
stages.narrative:
coarse whole wheat flour (atta), sooji (semolina), pure desi ghee, ajwain (carom seeds), panchmel dal (toor, chana, moong, urad, masoor), hing (asafoetida), cumin and mustard seeds, green chillies and ginger, jaggery or bura (powdered sugar), cardamom powder.

1. Prepare the baati dough: Mix coarse whole wheat flour, sooji, ajwain, salt, and melted ghee (moyen). Knead with warm water into a tight, firm dough. Rest for 20 minutes.
2. Shape the baatis: Pinch dough and roll into medium, smooth balls. Make a gentle thumb depression in the centre of each.
3. Bake the baatis: Arrange in a preheated baati oven, gas tandoor, or 200°C convection oven. Bake for 30–35 minutes, turning occasionally, until crisp and golden brown with cracked crusts.
4. Cook the Panchmel dal: Rinse and pressure-cook the five lentils with water, turmeric, and salt for 4 whistles until soft and creamy.
5. Temper the dal: Heat pure desi ghee in a pan; add cumin seeds, mustard seeds, hing, chopped green chillies, ginger, and red chilli powder. Pour the bubbling tadka over the cooked dal and simmer.
6. Make the churma: Take 4–5 hot baked baatis, crush them finely while warm (or pulse in a mixer), and pass through a coarse sieve.
7. Sweeten the churma: In a pan, warm a little ghee, add the crushed baati crumbs, powdered sugar (bura) or jaggery, and cardamom powder. Toss well and garnish with sliced almonds.
8. Serve hot: Gently crack each hot baati with your palms, submerge in a bowl of warm desi ghee, and serve on a royal thali with bubbling Panchmel dal, sweet churma, and garlic chutney.

stages.photoLabel: Laal Maas, Origin (Birth of the food)
stages.headline: Birth of Laal Maas in Rajasthan
stages.narrative: Laal maas ("red meat") is a fiery red meat curry of Rajasthan, said to have been cooked by Rajput royalty on hunting trips. Hunting parties carried few supplies, mainly chillies, garlic, yoghurt and rationed water, and marinated game such as wild boar, deer or jungle fowl in the camp kitchen. One legend says a Mewar king rejected deer meat cooked only with garlic and yoghurt because it smelled gamy, and the cook then added large amounts of chillies. Its red colour and heat come from Mathania chillies, grown near Mathania in Jodhpur. Sources date the dish to the 8th or the 10th century without evidence, so treat any date as unproven.

Traditional cookware: Camp pot or earthen pot.
Traditional heat source: Open wood fire in the hunting camp.
Cooking method: wild game (jungli maas) with chillies masking the gamy smell.
Ingredients known in this epoch: Wild game (boar, deer, jungle fowl), Mathania red chillies, Garlic, Yoghurt, Water.

stages.title: Recipe
stages.headline: Laal Maas Recipe: 8 Steps
stages.narrative:
mutton (goat meat with bone), Mathania dry red chillies, pure desi ghee, garlic paste, whisked curd (yoghurt), sliced onions, whole spices (cloves, black cardamom, cinnamon), coriander powder, turmeric, charcoal lump with cloves (for Dhungar smoke).

1. Prepare the chilli paste: Deseed Mathania red chillies, soak in warm water for 20 minutes, and grind into a smooth, vibrant red paste.
2. Marinate the mutton: Coat mutton pieces with half of the Mathania chilli paste, garlic paste, whisked curd, turmeric, and salt. Rest for 45 minutes.
3. Temper whole spices: Heat pure desi ghee generously in a heavy-bottomed handi; add black cardamom, green cardamom, cloves, cinnamon, and bay leaves until aromatic.
4. Brown the onions: Add finely sliced onions and sauté on medium heat until golden brown.
5. Bhuna the mutton: Add the marinated mutton and remaining garlic paste; roast on high heat for 10 minutes until the meat is seared and juices seal in.
6. Slow-simmer the curry: Add the remaining Mathania chilli paste, coriander powder, and a splash of warm water. Cover tightly and cook on low heat for 45–60 minutes until mutton is melt-in-mouth tender and ghee floats on top.
7. Infuse Dhungar smoke: Place a small metal bowl on the curry, add a red-hot charcoal piece, drop a clove and a spoonful of ghee over it, and seal the lid for 4 minutes to trap the royal campfire aroma.
8. Serve hot: Discard charcoal and serve the glistening scarlet curry with bajra roti, hot phulkas, or steamed rice.

stages.narrative: Rajasthan's deserts and princely courts developed water-sparse cooking, dried beans and berries, gram flour, ghee-rich sweets and slow-cooked meat curries. Ghewar is a sweet or dessert associated with Rajasthani sweet shops of Jaipur, Jodhpur and the monsoon-festival belt. Made for Teej and Raksha Bandhan and traditionally gifted to daughters and sisters. The dish is documented in regional cookery and food writing, but no securely dated earliest written reference has been established for it; this atlas therefore claims no century of invention.

stages.title: Origin
stages.headline: Birth of Sikkimese Momos in Sikkim & Trans-Himalayan Routes
stages.narrative: Sikkimese Momos trace their ancestral lineage to ancient Tibet and the historic trans-Himalayan trade routes connecting Lhasa, the Kathmandu Valley, and Sikkim through the high mountain passes of Nathu La and Jelep La. Derived from the Tibetan word 'mog mog', the art of steaming delicate parcels of unleavened flour dough filled with finely hand-minced highland meat and aromatics was brought to Sikkim by migrating Bhutia communities, Tibetan traders, and Newar merchants. Over generations, Sikkim adopted the dish as its paramount cultural and culinary emblem, adapting the filling to locally reared pork, beef, and indigenous mountain greens seasoned with wild mountain ginger and mountain garlic. Making momos evolved into an intimate communal ritual across Sikkimese households, where families gather in warmth around the hearth to knead, roll, pleat, and steam them over multi-tiered metal or bamboo steamers called 'moktu', served alongside blistering dalle khursani paste.

Cultural & family ritual: Making momos is an intimate communal ritual in Sikkim, bringing families together during cold Himalayan winters to pleat dough by hand.
Historical documentation: Rooted in Tibetan gastronomic archives and colonial travelogues detailing culinary exchange across the Chumbi Valley and Sikkim.

stages.title: Recipe
stages.photoLabel: Recipe (Sikkimese Steamed Momos Recipe: 10 Key Ingredients, 8 Steps)
stages.headline: Sikkimese Steamed Momos Recipe: 10 Key Ingredients, 8 Steps
stages.narrative:
Key ingredients: refined wheat flour (maida), minced pork or chicken, spring onions, fresh ginger, mountain garlic, black pepper powder, refined oil or pork lard, water, fiery dalle khursani chillies, local ripe tomatoes (for the dip).

1. In a large mixing bowl, combine wheat flour and a pinch of salt; gradually add room-temperature water and knead into a smooth, firm, and pliable dough.
2. Cover the kneaded dough with a moist cotton cloth and allow it to rest for at least 30 minutes to develop elasticity.
3. For the succulent filling, mix the minced meat with finely chopped spring onions, freshly minced ginger, crushed garlic, black pepper, and two tablespoons of oil or melted fat to retain juiciness.
4. Divide the rested dough into small equal cherry-sized balls; lightly flour your workstation and roll each ball into a very thin circular disc, keeping the edges slightly thinner than the center.
5. Place a rounded tablespoon of the savory filling directly in the center of the dough circle.
6. Carefully pleat the wrapper edges accordion-style in a half-moon or gathered top-knot purse, pinching tightly to create an airtight seal.
7. Lightly oil the perforated tiers of a traditional moktu (steamer) and arrange the pleated momos with adequate spacing to prevent sticking.
8. Stack the tiers over a vigorously boiling water base, cover with the domed lid, and steam on high flame for 10 to 12 minutes until translucent; serve piping hot with fire-roasted dalle khursani chutney.

stages.title: Origin
stages.headline: Birth of Gundruk Soup in Sikkim & Alpine Winter Preservation
stages.narrative: Gundruk is an ancient lactic-acid fermented leafy green preparation deeply rooted in the high-altitude agropastoral survival traditions of Sikkim's Nepali, Bhutia, and Lepcha communities. In the severe sub-zero winters of the Eastern Himalayas, heavy snowfalls historically halted all agricultural production, threatening mountain hamlets with severe nutrient and vitamin deficiencies. During the bountiful autumn harvest in October and November, rural households gathered the massive surplus of broadleaf mustard greens (rayo saag), radish leaves, and cauliflower foliage, wilted them under the autumn sun, crushed them, and tightly tamped them into earthen jars (dhungro) or underground pits without salt. Wild lactobacillus bacteria naturally fermented the leaves into a pleasantly sour, mineral-rich preserved food, which was then sun-dried and stored for up to a year. Rehydrated and cooked with tomatoes, garlic, and mustard oil, Gundruk Soup (Gundruk ko Jhol) became Sikkim's ultimate restorative alpine broth, revered for its digestive warmth and sour, earthy profile.
details: Origin in Sikkim: Born from centuries-old alpine winter survival strategies of mountain farming communities across the Sikkimese Himalayas.
Cultural & communal ritual: Harvested and preserved in late autumn; shared among neighboring households as a cherished emblem of Himalayan mutual aid.
Historical documentation: Recorded in Eastern Himalayan ethnographic studies and folklore documenting salt-free lactic fermentation in earthen jars.
Curative broth: Slow-simmered with mountain garlic, tomatoes, and mustard oil into a tangy, probiotic, mineral-dense soup served with steamed rice.
stages.evidenceNote: Himalayan ethno-microbiological and historical accounts record centuries-old pit and earthen-jar lactic fermentation of leafy greens across Sikkim.

stages.title: Recipe
stages.photoLabel: Recipe (Sikkimese Gundruk Soup Recipe: 10 Key Ingredients, 8 Steps)
stages.headline: Sikkimese Gundruk Soup Recipe: 10 Key Ingredients, 8 Steps
stages.narrative:
Key ingredients: authentic dried gundruk (fermented mustard/radish greens), pure cold-pressed mustard oil, medium onion, fresh garlic cloves, fresh ginger, ripe country tomatoes, dried red chillies or dalle khursani, parched local soybeans (bhatmas) or potato, turmeric powder, fresh coriander leaves.

1. Take authentic dried gundruk greens and soak them in lukewarm water for 15 to 20 minutes until softened and rehydrated.
2. Squeeze the excess water gently from the rehydrated greens, coarsely chop them with a kitchen knife, and set aside.
3. Heat cold-pressed mustard oil in a heavy-bottomed pot until it smokes lightly, then lower heat to temper the pungent aroma.
4. Add whole dried red chillies (or slit dalle khursani) and sauté until they turn deep red and aromatic.
5. Add chopped onions, minced garlic, and grated ginger; fry on medium flame until golden-brown and fragrant.
6. Stir in chopped ripe tomatoes, turmeric powder, and salt; cook down for 3 to 4 minutes until the tomatoes form a soft, pulpy masala base.
7. Add the chopped gundruk and roasted soybeans (bhatmas); stir-fry together for 3 minutes to infuse the greens with the aromatics.
8. Pour in three cups of water, bring to a vigorous boil, then cover and simmer over low heat for 15 minutes to yield a tangy, earthy broth; garnish with fresh coriander and serve hot with steamed rice.

stages.title: Origin
stages.photoLabel: Idli Sambar - Origin (Birth of the food)
stages.headline: Birth of Idli and Sambar in South Indian Traditions
stages.narrative: Idli sambar is a South Indian meal of steamed idlis (soft cakes of fermented rice and black gram batter) served with sambar, a lentil and tamarind vegetable stew. It is eaten across South India and is closely linked with Tamil Nadu. Idli: the earliest mentions are in Kannada and Sanskrit texts of the 9th to 13th centuries. These include Vaddaradhane (c. 920 CE, "iddalige") and Manasollasa (1130 CE, "iddarika"). Those early versions are described as made from black gram, without rice, without long fermentation and without steaming. The modern idli is mentioned only from about 1250 CE onwards. Food historian K. T. Achaya has suggested that the steamed idli may have reached India from present-day Indonesia (a dish called "kedli") between 800 and 1200 CE. Others argue that batter fermentation developed independently in India. A third theory credits Arab traders. These are theories, and none is settled. Sambar: an early reference to a similar dish appears in the Telugu poem Amuktamalyada (c. 1517). Another appears in a Kannada text of 1648 (Kanthirava Narasaraja Vijaya), which describes a similar curry of vegetables and toor dal. A popular legend says sambar was first made in the Thanjavur Maratha court (in the time of Shahuji I) and named after Sambhaji. Historians treat this as a story, not proven history. The exact origin, date and creator of idli and of sambar are not documented with certainty.

stages.title: Recipe
stages.headline: Idli Sambar Recipe: 8 Steps
stages.narrative:
idli rice (parboiled rice), whole black gram (urad dal), fenugreek seeds, salt, toor dal, tamarind, mixed vegetables (drumstick, carrot, brinjal, potato), shallots or onion and tomato, sambar powder with turmeric, mustard seeds, curry leaves and asafoetida (hing).

1. Soak the rice and dal. Wash the idli rice, and soak it separately from the black gram and fenugreek for a few hours. (The grains should be soft enough to press between two fingers.)
2. Grind the batter. Grind the black gram and fenugreek with a little water until light and fluffy, then grind the rice more coarsely. (The black gram batter should look airy and smooth, and the rice batter slightly grainy.)
3. Ferment the batter. Mix the two batters with salt and leave the batter covered in a warm place overnight. (It is ready when it has risen and smells mildly sour.)
4. Steam the idlis. Grease the idli plates, pour in the batter and steam over boiling water for about 10 to 15 minutes. (A knife pushed in should come out clean.)
5. Cook the dal. Pressure cook the toor dal with turmeric until it is very soft, then mash it lightly. (It should look creamy with no whole grains.)
6. Cook the vegetables. Fry shallots or onion and tomato, add the vegetables and cook until they soften. (They should be soft but still hold their shape.)
7. Make the sambar. Add tamarind extract, salt and sambar powder to the vegetables, stir in the dal and simmer. (The raw smell of the tamarind should go, and the sambar should thicken slightly.)
8. Temper and serve. Splutter mustard seeds, curry leaves and hing in hot oil, pour it over the sambar and serve it with the hot idlis. (The sambar should smell fragrant. Serve while the idlis are still soft and steaming.)

1. Soak the rice and dal. Wash the idli rice, and soak it separately from the black gram and fenugreek for a few hours. (The grains should be soft enough to press between two fingers.)

3. Ferment the batter. Mix the two batters with salt and leave the batter covered in a warm place overnight. (It is ready when it has risen and smells mildly sour.)
4. Steam the idlis. Grease the idli plates, pour in the batter and steam over boiling water for about 10 to 15 minutes. (A knife pushed in should come out clean.)

8. Temper and serve. Splutter mustard seeds, curry leaves and hing in hot oil, pour it over the sambar and serve it with the hot idlis. (The sambar should smell fragrant. Serve while the idlis are still soft and steaming.)

stages.title: Origin
stages.photoLabel: Filter Coffee - Origin (Birth of the food)
stages.headline: Birth of Filter Coffee in South India
stages.narrative: Filter coffee (filter kaapi) is a South Indian drink of strong coffee decoction mixed with hot milk and sugar. It is made in a two-part metal filter and served in a steel tumbler and dabara. It is popular across Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Kerala and Andhra Pradesh, and is especially linked with Tamil households. A popular belief says a Sufi named Baba Budan brought seven coffee beans from the Middle East (accounts say Mecca or Yemen) and planted them in the Chandragiri hills of Chikmagalur, Karnataka. This is widely told as a belief and is not established fact. Sources place it in the 16th or the 17th century, and they do not agree. Coffee was expensive at first. Cultivation was promoted in the colonial era, and the drink moved from the elite to ordinary people. By the early 20th century, filter coffee was a staple in homes, restaurants and roadside stalls. Chicory, a roasted ground root, was added to the coffee. Sources say it gives body and a bold flavour. Outlook Traveller says it was reportedly added for medicinal reasons. The Indian Coffee House, which emerged in the mid-20th century, helped carry coffee to northern India. The exact origin, date and creator of filter coffee are not documented with certainty.

stages.title: Recipe
stages.headline: Filter Coffee Recipe: 8 Steps
stages.narrative:
filter coffee powder (medium to dark roast), chicory (blended into the powder), freshly boiled water, full-cream milk, sugar (or jaggery).

1. Set up the filter. Place the upper cup of the filter on the lower cup. (The perforated base should sit flat with no gaps.)
2. Add the coffee powder. Put the coffee-chicory powder into the upper cup and press it gently with the disc. (Press lightly, because packing it too hard slows the drip too much.)
3. Add boiling water. Pour freshly boiled water over the powder and put the lid on. (The water must be boiling, not just warm.)
4. Let the decoction drip. Leave it for about 10 to 15 minutes. (The decoction should collect in the lower cup as a thick, dark liquid. Do not leave it much beyond 20 minutes, or it turns bitter.)
5. Heat the milk. Warm full-cream milk on the stove until it is hot. (It should be steaming, and not boiled over.)
6. Mix the coffee. Pour a little decoction into the tumbler, add the hot milk and sugar, and stir. (The colour should be a rich brown. Adjust the decoction and milk to taste.)
7. Aerate the coffee. Pour the coffee back and forth between the tumbler and the dabara in a high arc. (It should turn frothy and cool to a drinkable temperature.)
8. Serve. Set the tumbler in the dabara and serve at once. (Serve it hot, while the froth is still on top.)

stages.narrative: Biryani traces back to Persian and Mughal rice-and-meat dishes that came into the Deccan. Hyderabadi biryani developed under the Asaf Jahi (Nizam) rulers and their royal kitchens, combining Mughal cooking with local Deccan ingredients and tastes. The exact date and creator are not documented with certainty, and several origin stories exist. It is cooked in the dum method (sealed pot, slow steam). The kacchi style, with raw marinated meat, is the best known Hyderabadi version.

stages.title: Recipe
stages.headline: Hyderabadi Dum Biryani Recipe: 8 Steps
stages.narrative:
basmati rice, mutton or chicken, curd, fried onions, ginger-garlic paste, green chillies, whole spices and garam masala, mint and coriander, saffron milk, ghee.

1. Marinate the meat with curd, spices, ginger-garlic paste, herbs and fried onions. Mix well and rest it (overnight for best flavour, or a few hours).
2. Fry the onions until golden brown and crisp. Keep some aside for layering.
3. Parboil the rice with whole spices and salt until about 70% cooked (the grain should break easily but still feel firm inside). Drain it.
4. Layer the marinated meat at the bottom of a heavy pot, then spread the rice evenly on top.
5. Top with fried onions, mint, coriander, saffron milk and ghee.
6. Seal the lid tightly with dough or foil so no steam escapes.
7. Cook on high heat for a few minutes until steam builds, then on low heat for about 40 minutes (dum).
8. Rest for 10 minutes without opening, then mix gently from the sides and serve with raita.

stages.title: Origin
stages.headline: Birth of Hyderabadi Haleem in Telangana & the Deccan
stages.narrative: Haleem traces its ancestry to the medieval Arab dish harees, a slow-cooked porridge of pounded meat and wheat. It was introduced to Hyderabad by the Arab diaspora (Chaush soldiers from Yemen) serving in the irregular army of the Asaf Jahi Nizams. In the royal kitchens of the Nizams and Paigah nobles, the rustic harees was refined and Indianized by introducing aromatic Deccan spices, mixed lentils, ghee, dry fruits, and rose petals. It became the signature delicacy of Hyderabad, especially cherished during Ramzan for breaking the fast.
details: Origin in Telangana: Haleem traces its ancestry to the medieval Arab dish harees, brought to Hyderabad by Yemeni Chaush soldiers serving the Asaf Jahi Nizams.
Royal court refinement: In the royal kitchens of the Nizams and Paigah nobles, the rustic harees was refined with local Deccan spices, mixed lentils, pure ghee, dry fruits, and rose petals.
Cultural tradition: Cooked overnight in large wood-fired copper degs and served as the preeminent energy-replenishing dish to break the fast during Ramzan.
Cooking method: Slow-simmered for 8 to 12 hours and vigorously pounded with heavy wooden pestles (ghotni) until meat and wheat merge into a smooth, cohesive porridge.

stages.title: Recipe
stages.headline: Hyderabadi Haleem Recipe: 8 Steps
stages.narrative:
broken wheat (dalia), boneless mutton, chana and moong lentils, curd, pure desi ghee, fried onions (birista), ginger-garlic paste, whole spices and garam masala, mint and coriander, almonds and cashew nuts.

1. Soak broken wheat and lentils (chana and moong) in water for 1 to 2 hours, then drain.
2. Marinate the mutton with curd, ginger-garlic paste, turmeric, chilli powder, salt, and half of the garam masala for at least 1 hour.
3. In a heavy pot or pressure cooker, heat ghee and saute whole spices (shahi jeera, cardamom, cloves, cinnamon) and a portion of fried onions until fragrant.
4. Add the marinated meat and sear on medium-high heat, then add water and pressure-cook or slow-simmer until the meat is thoroughly tender and falling apart.
5. Separately boil the soaked broken wheat and lentils with a pinch of turmeric and water until completely soft and mushy.
6. Shred the cooked meat off any bones and combine the shredded meat and its rich broth into the pot of cooked wheat and lentils.
7. Slow-simmer over low heat while vigorously mashing and pounding with a wooden masher (ghotni) for 30–40 minutes, gradually incorporating hot ghee until the mixture turns silky, elastic, and pasty.
8. Season with remaining garam masala, mint, and coriander; ladle into warm bowls and top with hot ghee, golden fried onions, toasted cashews, and fresh lemon wedges.

stages.narrative: Telangana's Deccan plateau and Hyderabad's courtly kitchens combine millets, rice, slow-cooked meat and wheat stews with Persianate sweets and biryanis. Qubani ka Meetha is a sweet or dessert associated with Hyderabad's Deccani kitchens, drawing on Central Asian dried-fruit cookery. A wedding and banquet dessert that made imported dried apricots into a local sweet. The dish is documented in regional cookery and food writing, but no securely dated earliest written reference has been established for it; this atlas therefore claims no century of invention.

stages.title: Origin
stages.headline: Birth of Mui Borok in the Manikya Kingdom & Borok Forest Hearth
details: Origin among the Borok people: Mui Borok (meaning 'Borok Curry' in the indigenous Kokborok language) is the foundational culinary staple of the Tripuri people, celebrated throughout the history of the Manikya dynasty.

The soul of 'Berma': Central to Mui Borok is 'Berma'—sun-dried, naturally fermented small river fish packed into earthen jars (taler) and matured for months to yield an intensely savory, umami-rich paste.
Zero-oil health philosophy: Prepared entirely without cooking oil, the dish highlights the pristine flavours of fresh freshwater catch, mountain green chillies, garlic, and wild herbs.
Cooking method: River fish is stewed in spring water with berma, crushed ginger, garlic, and green chillies in earthenware pots, finished with fragrant wild lemon basil leaves.

River fish is stewed in spring water with berma, crushed ginger, garlic, and green chillies in earthenware pots, finished with fragrant wild lemon basil leaves.

stages.headline: Mui Borok Recipe: 10 Key Ingredients, 8 Steps
chips: Fresh local river fish (chanda or rohu steaks)
Tender seasonal vegetables (eggplant or bamboo shoots)
details: Key ingredients: fresh local river fish (chanda or rohu steaks), berma (traditional fermented dried fish paste), fresh green hill chillies, fresh ginger paste, crushed garlic cloves, wild coriander leaves (khundrupwi), fresh lemon basil leaves, tender seasonal vegetables (eggplant or bamboo shoots), pinch of turmeric powder, sea salt and spring water.
1. Clean freshwater fish steaks thoroughly under running water, rub with a pinch of turmeric and salt, and set aside.
2. Cut local tender eggplant or bamboo shoots into bite-sized segments; crush fresh ginger, garlic cloves, and green hill chillies coarsely in a mortar.
3. In a small bowl, dissolve 2 tablespoons of traditional berma paste in 1/2 cup of warm water, straining lightly to ensure smooth dispersion.
4. In an earthenware pot or deep saucepan, bring 2.5 cups of filtered spring water to a rolling boil over medium-high heat.
5. Pour the dissolved berma mixture into the boiling water along with crushed ginger, garlic, green chillies, and sea salt, boiling for 5 minutes until intensely fragrant.
6. Add the tender seasonal vegetables into the bubbling broth and cook for 4 minutes until half-cooked.
7. Gently slide the fresh fish steaks into the boiling broth, lower the flame to medium, and simmer uncovered for 6 to 8 minutes until the fish is tender and fully infused.
8. Toss in torn wild coriander leaves (khundrupwi) and fresh lemon basil leaves, remove from heat immediately, cover for 2 minutes to trap the aroma, and serve hot with steamed white rice.

details: Origin in ancient Tripuri botany: Chakhwi is a revered ancestral delicacy of the Borok (Tripuri) people, built around the sophisticated use of natural plant-ash alkaline water known as 'Khar' or 'Khang'.

Cooking method: Sliced bamboo shoots and pork are simmered in the khar filtrate with ginger, green chillies, and berma, lightly thickened with a spoonful of rice flour paste.
